Treehouse — design & build

Great Lakes region · studies, the construction set and the experience

Studies answer “should we?” They are illustrative, they may show options that were never adopted, and they must never be measured from. Each one is frozen at the datum it was drawn against — it is a dated record of what was known when a decision was made, so it is not refreshed when the design moves. For what is actually being built, see the Drawings tab.

The SOUTH gable, framed — R41's arrangement, drawn

Gable studs stacked over wall studs at 16 o.c., the rough 4×4 ring plate as the visual band, sheathed — ⭐ the aesthetic IS the code condition (stacking makes R602.3.2's ≤ 1-in offset zero). ⭐⭐ THE FIND: the triangle the framing makes is not register G-1's — its top boundary is the roof SHEATHING plane, a constant 5.0–7.3 in lift — so the RULED G-A window gains 12 % of glass, all in height, free (872 → 975 in²) and the ruling survives its own correction. The south gable, framed

R41 adopted an arrangement in one sentence and asked to see it. This is that sentence drawn — wall studs at 16 in o.c. below, the rough true 4×4 ring plate as a horizontal band, gable studs standing on it on the same centres, bevel-cut to a raked cap at the sheathing plane. Drawing it turned up four things the sentence did not contain, one of which moves a figure the register calls decided.

THE BRIEF, VERBATIM (owner, R41, 2026-08-16):
“dimensional gable studs stacked above wall studs broken visually horizontally by 4x rough top plate. 16 oc same as wall studs so gable and wall studs look ‘continuous’; disappear into top plate but then reappear on journey up to the ceiling. sheathed.”

⭐ The aesthetic IS the code condition. The 2021 IRC R602.3.2 single-top-plate exception wants the framing above a single plate to sit over the studs below within 1 in. Stacking makes that offset zero. The look the owner described and the compliance route are the same discipline — which is why one drawing answers both, and why the arrangement is worth confirming rather than merely permitting.

① The elevation — the owner's line, drawn

The stud line runs from the sole plate to the plate underside at 5'-2", disappears behind 4" of rough true 4×4, and reappears on the same centres above it. The two gable-line plate segments (5'-6 1/2" + 3'-1 1/2") side-frame the continuous S-gable ridge post (J14); the corners over the R30 posts are J13. Neither joint is specified — both are PE TO CONFIRM.

⭐⭐ THE TRIANGLE THE FRAMING MAKES IS NOT THE TRIANGLE THE REGISTER MEASURES. Register G-1 (DECIDED 2026-08-10) rules gable heights off the slope-defining triangle — drawn dashed above — and its stated reason is that it closes on the plate at both wall lines at exactly 0.0000. The framed triangle does not close there at all: its top boundary is the roof sheathing plane, which stands 5.03 in above the plate at the SW corner and 7.27 in at the SE. Two different surfaces have been carrying one name.

The gap is not an error in either place — it is the eave seats plus the rafter's own plumb depth. West: the soffit plane passes through the plate top 2 1/2" inboard of the wall line and the rafter is 7.003 in deep measured plumb. East: 1 1/2" and 9.316 in on the steeper plane, which is why that corner stands higher. NEEDS_CONTEXT — owner. G-1's own words say “gable heights” without saying which question they answer, and for anything framed inside this triangle the framed surface is the binding one.

⭐ AND THE DIFFERENCE IS A CONSTANT, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES IT SAFE TO ABSORB. Both surfaces are planes at the same pitch, so the offset does not vary along the rake: on the west plane the framed sheathing plane runs a flat 5.033 in above G-1's line everywhere, and the buildable surface — under a raked cap laid flat — a flat 3.123 in; on the east plane, 7.265 and 4.725 in. The correction is a uniform lift, not a change of shape, which is exactly why every width sized off G-1 keeps its proportions and simply gains head-room — and why the ruled window's own width survives below. (The generator asserts the offset is constant at five stations; if that ever fails this paragraph is wrong, not stale.)

The ruled window, and what the correction does to it

⛔ THE 1.2c/1.2d PAIR IS SUPERSEDED AND IS NOT DRAWN AS A CANDIDATE. R18 (owner, 2026-08-13) ruled the south above-loft opening a single fixed pane west of the ridge post — G-A, 33.25 × 26.21 — and the same-day EAST reopening left the SOUTH half standing confirmed. What this page raises

  1. ⭐⭐ G-1's construction and the framed triangle are different surfaces (5.03 / 7.27 in at the corners). Everything sized in this triangle off G-1 has that much more room than it was sized against. NEEDS_CONTEXT — owner; the register row is DECIDED and this page does not re-rule it.
  2. ⚠ The raked cap's orientation is unstated and expensive (85 in² of glass, and the entire corner condition). NEEDS_CONTEXT — PE, with P10, which is the same detail seen from the diaphragm side: the cap is the roof sheathing's boundary member at this edge.
  3. ⛔ G-A's east jamb IS the loaded S-gable ridge post (271.6 lb, continuous floor to ridge soffit, seated on J12 — PE TO CONFIRM). R18 chose SE-3 hard-east below the loft precisely to delete the ridge-post/king-stud question; above the loft, G-A re-creates it. PE.
  4. ⚠ Build-guide 2.11 is one datum generation behind. Its table prices the E & W plate as a doubled 2×4 reading WHITE, and its section 2 invents a 0.50-in facing board to carry the timber band round a corner it says the band dies at. R5 made that plate a single rough TRUE 4×4 — TIMBER by 2.11's own rule — and R32 put the same member on this gable line, so the band the owner is asking to see is already structural and the facing board is solving a problem the datum dissolved. The band does still stop — at the NORTH, because R35c deleted the station-16 segments. Domain C.
  5. ⚠ The stud layout ORIGIN is stated by no source. Drawn from the west wall line on the sheathing module, which puts the balance bay (11 1/4") at the east end. Which end carries it decides whether G-A's jambs land on the module, and it is an owner/field call, not a drafting one.
  6. ⬇ Does the SOUTH triangle get its own operable vent? R38 gave the station-43.5 triangle a closable screened vent for summer airflow. This gable is the other end of the same roof cavity, and a single vent is half a path. OPEN — owner question, not asked here and not answered here; any vent is an operable opening and lands in the enclosure inventory (ASCE 7-16 §26.2), which is a PE line.
  7. ⛔ No header depth and no rough-versus-net-clear allowance exist on file for this opening — the frozen south-wall-openings study raised both and neither has been answered. Nothing is sized here.
The verdict on the arrangement itself: it draws cleanly, it is the conventional gable-endwall detail for the condition (full-height gable studs on a raked cap — AWC Guide to Wood Construction in High Wind Areas §4.2, Fig. 10 + Table 5; the hinge-at-the-plate-line failure FEMA P-804 §4.2 exists to retrofit is answered here by continuity at construction), its 16-in module clears the continuous ridge post at every station, and it delivers the horizontal timber band the interior finish document was building a workaround to fake. Nothing found argues against it. The seven items above are what it costs to draw it honestly, and the owner rules every one of them.

One larger east window — instead of two

On 2026-08-13 R18 ruled a four-window programme, and the same day the owner reopened its east half: “i like the idea of one larger e window rather than two on east”. So the ruled pair — the centred 24 × 24 squeeze window plus a contiguous 16 in high band, 40 in of opening — is now the reference, and this page asks what one hole can do instead in the 94.5 in of wall between the north trimmer and the south gable line. The answer turns on one thing the pair could not use: a single centred opening leaves two EQUAL segments, and the shear-wall engine derates the short one.

⛔ NOTHING ON THIS PAGE IS SELECTED. Register 1.2 records the R18 programme as ruled; the EAST half is REOPENED (memo, same day) pending this study, and the SOUTH half stands confirmed. What survives the reopening unchanged is the exit role: register 1.2a migrated it on 2026-08-13, so the SOUTH SE-3 window is the second means of egress of record and the east opening is the deliberate below-reference supplementary escape. Its sill remains deliberately unset pending the PE’s fall-protection read (cover email §1.4). Every single window here is a dashed candidate with its arithmetic beside it.

① The wall as R18 left it

At the same 40 inches of opening, one centred hole takes 13 % OFF the pair’s governing utilisation — and the saving is exactly the ratio of the two aspect-ratio factors. The pair splits the wall 19.25 / 35.25; one centred window of the same width splits it 27.25 / 27.25. Σb is identical at 54.5 in, so the unit shear is identical too — but the pair’s short piece is derated to ARF 0.8214 while both balanced pieces sit at 0.9472, and the derated one governs. 1.159 → 1.005 under the couple; 0.795 → 0.689 with the R16 nailing. The generator asserts that the improvement equals the ARF ratio and nothing else — if anything else moved, the explanation would be wrong.

③ How wide can one window be

⭐ The bound below is unchanged by the 2026-08-13 revision and is kept as the labelled bound it always was. What the revision did was name three finalists inside it; the curve, the 52.84 in crossing and the 56.79 in aspect cap are exactly as first derived.

The widest single window that closes is 52.84 in — and it is the mechanism that stops it, not the geometry. Two constraints could have bound. The aspect limit kills a segment below h/3.5 = 18.86 in, which would have allowed 56.79 in of opening. The §14.7 couple with the adopted R16 nailing crosses 1.000 first, at 52.84 in — 3.95 in short of it. Round down and 52 in is the widest whole inch that closes (0.971). ⚠ Without the R16 upgrade the same curve crosses at 39.77 in, so the adopted nailing is worth 13.06 in of window — and the pair’s own 40 in would have sat just outside it (0.23 in over). The solve is done in closed form and again by bisection on the drawn curve; the generator refuses the page unless the two agree to 1e−9.

④ ⑤ Windows onto rafter tails — the head-height question

⭐ The owner’s reading, 2026-08-13: “can we move two surviving options slightly below top plate; as currently stands it seems like these will be windows onto rafter tails…”

He is right, and it is the steep plane that does it. The east roof rises at 1.367 against the west’s 0.788, so outboard of this wall the eave drops away fast — and every head on figures ① and ② is drawn at the plate underside, which is the one place where the tail is directly overhead. The v8 taper lifts the tip back up: the tail underside at the 15 in eave tip derives to 49.37 in above the floor datum (⚠️ on EAVE_OVERHANG_NOMINAL — NOMINAL, FIELD VERIFY), against 43.44 without it.
The tails band is set by the HEAD alone. Width changes nothing; height changes only what fraction of the glass it is. At a given head and a given standing distance, every candidate on this page shows the same number of inches of tail — because the eave cuts the view at one height at the wall plane, and the head is the only thing above it. So the answer to “windows onto rafter tails” is the head, and only the head. At 2 ft back, dropping from 62 to 54 takes the tails band from 8.54 in to 0.54 in; at 1 ft it goes to nothing at all. And it is solved twice — a closed form and a bisection on a ray marched along the real tapered underside — which must agree before the page may be written.

At a 60 in ILLUSTRATIVE eye — ⛔ no project source states an eye height; register 0.4’s convention is a 6 ft adult, a working stature and not a code figure, and the same-date porch-trunk-view study carries the same 60 in reference with the same disclosure. Standing distances are measured west of the wall line and stop at the ridge, because a standpoint further west looks out under the west plane, the ridge beam and the loft — none of which this section models. Geometry from geometry.py: TAN_E, EAVE_SEAT_E, EAVE_OVERHANG_NOMINAL, RAFTER_TAIL_TIP_D, TAIL_TIP_RISE_E, PLUMB_E — DATUM v9, taper rule DATUM v8 A/C.

A standing adult sees no open sky through this wall at all — and the hinge is the tail tip’s own height, from any distance. The ray that grazes the tip crosses the eye’s own level only when the eye is at 49.37 in, the height of the tip itself, and that is true at every standing distance — the distance cancels. So an eye above 49.37 sees only tail above its own level and only ground below it; an eye below it always keeps a band of open sky. A 60 in eye is above the hinge; a seated or a child’s eye is not. ⛔ What actually occupies the open air — sky, canopy, the oak, the meadow — is not modelled, and nothing here claims a view of anything. The level ray is drawn because it is exact: it separates looking up from looking down.
⚠ What a lower head costs, stated straight.
  • A lower head is a lower sill, inch for inch, at a fixed glass height. On this ladder the finalists’ sills run E-S1 32/28/24 · E-S1b 38/34/30 · E-S3 38/34/30 (inches above the floor, at heads 62/58/54). ⛔ Every one of them is below the 42 in kid band of register 0.3a — the highest sill any finalist reaches at any head on this ladder is 38, which is 4 in short of it. The sill stays deliberately unset pending the PE’s fall-protection read, exactly as the cover letter puts it; this page measures the gap and does not close it.
  • ⭐ E-S1b is on the page for precisely this trade. It is E-S1 to the last digit in every structural column, and six inches shorter — so at every head it drops the head away from the soffit and keeps the sill six inches higher, at once. That is the one thing a shorter window buys, and it costs 240 in² of aperture.
  • A head below the plate underside needs short cripple studs between the header and the plate — ordinary framing, and nothing more. ⛔ This page sizes neither cripple nor header: no source states a header depth for these openings. What it can say is arithmetic: dropping the head frees 0/4/8 in above it, and the header tab’s own trial section is 7.25 in deep — so of the three, only head 54 leaves room for a section of that depth. ⭐ Read the other way round, the ladder is not a new ask at all: a real header under a 62 in plate underside puts the head near 54.75 anyway.
  • Shear does not see any of it. Every column in the table above is unchanged at every head — the segmented method counts full-height segments, so an opening costs its full width whatever its sill or its head. The generator re-prices every candidate at every head and refuses the page if a single figure moves.

Height, honestly: shear-free, but not free

⭐ Nothing in the shear arithmetic sees height. The segmented method counts full-height segments, so an opening costs its full width whatever its sill — every column above would be identical if each candidate were half as tall or twice. That is why the option set varies width and leaves height to the two lines that actually bound it.

⚠ But height is not header-free either, and it costs in two different directions.
  • WIDER costs a longer header. The header span is the opening plus the tab’s own bearing allowance (4 in) — ⚠️ not the opening width, which is what a first reading assumes. Across this whole option set the header’s governing check stays NOTCHED SHEAR @ combo 3 D+S and rises in a straight line with span: 32 in → 0.192; 40 in → 0.234; 48 in → 0.277; 52 in → 0.298. The tab’s own trial section (a doubled 2× at 3 × 7.25) would not reach 1.000 until a span of about 188 in — longer than the wall. ⭐ So no candidate here needs more than the doubled-2×8 basis, and the header is nowhere the binding constraint. ⛔ That is evidence about this class of opening on this wall, not a header specification for anything drawn here.
    Basis: register 1.2a (R12/R13, exit role migrated by R18) · CALC: 9_TH_HDR_EXIT_E, an instance of 3_ENG_BEAM — re-run here at other spans and checked against its own four rows at its own span.
  • TALLER costs sill, and the header takes the top. Both height figures on figure ① are measured to the plate underside (62). The two sill lines leave a two-inch band, and everything taller than 20 in is a request to the PE. That is exactly the tension the letter already puts to the PE in its own words: “its sill is deliberately unset pending your read — our standing rule elevates operable glazing to 42 in for the kids, the egress function pulls the other way”. ⛔ This page measures it; it does not resolve it.

⚠ Where this arithmetic could be wrong, in either direction

In the wall’s favour — the engine is SEGMENTED-ONLY. 9_TH_SW_E’s SCOPE note: “SEGMENTED WALLS ONLY (SDPWS 4.3.5.1…). No perforated shear wall (4.3.5.3…) and no force-transfer-around-openings wall (4.3.5.2).” Both methods exist to credit sheathing above and below an opening — and a single large window leaves a continuous strip above and below it, which is exactly what they credit. ⭐ So these prices are the conservative ones, and a force-transfer treatment is the one route that could widen the window further. But not by an amount anyone may assume, and choosing a method is a PE-and-workbook decision, not a study’s.

Against it — this line’s share is held FIXED while its Σb changes. The SCOPE note also says “NO SHEAR-WALL-LINE DISTRIBUTION (4.3.3.4)”, so every candidate here changes this wall’s Σb and nothing else. A real distribution would move force between EAST and WEST as one of them is opened, and which way depends on the diaphragm.

And the couple column is not a ceiling. §14.7 brackets four mechanisms; the couple is the one that lands on this wall. Row 3 — two-support beam equilibrium, the row that satisfies moment equilibrium about a real point — puts CHASE-SOUTH at util 1.69 and drives SOUTH into reversal instead. The bracket is a band, not a worst case for every member at once.

And the R16 nailing is adopted, but its spacing is not. R16 takes the tighter Table 4.3A row as the design intent; which row (4 in or 3 in) is selected from this study’s own third column at the calcs bind, and the memo is explicit that the tight-spacing footnote is read from the on-file table “not assumed either way”. The workbook says the same about its own bind, and it is worth reading in full rather than in summary:

“MANDATORY CAVEAT, AND IT IS NOT A FORMALITY: Table 4.3A’s tighter-spacing rows carry FOOTNOTE CONDITIONS on framing width at abutting panel edges, fastener edge distance and panel layout, and THOSE FOOTNOTES ARE NOT TRANSCRIBED ANYWHERE ON FILE. This tab has bound the CAPACITY. It has NOT established that the wall can be BUILT to the row it now claims … If the footnote conditions are not met this capacity is not available and the wall reverts to the 6-in row.”

So column C’s ratio is the table’s and its buildability at this framing is not on file — and if it proves unavailable, every candidate here is read out of column B instead, where only E-S3 closes.
Quoted from 4_ENG_SW’s own R16 note, located by its row label on the recalculated workbook.

Deliberately NOT drawn

  • A choice, a recommendation, or an adopted width or height. The east half of R18 is reopened and this page is an input to re-ruling it.
  • A sill. The letter states it is unset pending the PE’s fall-protection read; this page draws the two lines that bound it.
  • A header depth or a header specification. The 7.25 in figure is the calc tab’s own trial section, used to show what a header would take out of the opening height — no source states one.
  • An adopted mechanism. The couple is the workbook’s row 4 of four, quoted; the ruling is the PE’s, over an open-front condition whose governing provisions are believed applicable and not transcribed.
  • A nailing SPACING, or any claim that the tighter row’s framing and edge-distance conditions are met.
  • Any glazing product, sash type, operation, opening-control device, hardware or glass specification, and no frame/sash allowance — none is on file, so no candidate can be said to meet or miss any reference figure.
  • Any code-compliance verdict. The SDPWS numbers are the workbook’s transcription; the utilisations are ours, not a licensed engineer’s. IRC-class figures appear only as [REG] REFERENCE, NOT ADOPTED (0.1b).
  • New wind arithmetic of any kind, and no utilisation at any plate height other than R14’s ruled one.
  • A perforated or force-transfer-around-openings treatment. Named as the route that could widen the window, not run.
  • Hold-down hardware, and no deflection figure — 9_TH_SW_E’s is flagged NOT QUOTABLE.
  • Anything on the SOUTH wall. Its half of R18 stands confirmed and has its own study of the same date.
  • A HEAD HEIGHT. 62/58/54 is a ladder the owner asked to see, not a schedule. ⛔ Nothing on this page selects one.
  • An EYE HEIGHT as fact, a stature, or any child figure. The 60 in eye is ILLUSTRATIVE and labelled so everywhere it is drawn; the whole sweep is on the page.
  • Any claim about what is actually visible out of the window. The geometry says where the eave cuts the sightline; sky, canopy, the oak and the meadow are none of them in this datum.
  • A cripple-stud or header SIZE. A head below the plate underside needs short cripples — ordinary framing, named and not sized.
  • A re-derivation of anything the owner set aside. The record section carries the same figures the lead comparison carried before the revision.

Two windows on the south wall — above and below the loft

One wall, cut in two by the loft, with opposite economics either side of the top plate. Above it the gable triangle is not part of the shear wall at all, so a window there costs zero Σb. Below it is a counted E–W shear line at 0.293, and that is the margin the ruled egress window is spent out of. Above the loft the question is shape; below it the question is width, and where along the wall.

Every opening on this page is a dashed candidate with its arithmetic beside it.

① The whole wall, both windows

Above the loft, the biggest single pane is not the most glass. The ridge post splits the gable into unequal halves: a 66.5 in west run and a 37.5 in east one. The best single rectangle on the west side is 33.25 × 26.21 — 872 in², 1.81× the best one on the east. But register 1.2c’s pair, each at its own peak, is 961 in² of glass — 1.10× the single. One big window or two smaller ones is a look decision, and both are free.

② Above the loft

⚠ An above-loft window is at KID HEIGHT for anyone ON the loft — and nobody has ruled what that means. Every gable rectangle sits on the plate line, 66 in above the room’s floor. The loft deck is at 54, so the same sill is 12 in above the floor a child is actually on. Register 0.3a governs glazing that can open or break and sets the band at 42 in — but it does not say from which floor.
  • Read from the room floor, the whole gable is above the band and every option is available.
  • Read from the loft floor, the band lands 30 in above the plate, and the free window shrinks to 14.22 × 11.21 west (159 in², 18% of G-A) or 7.78 × 10.63 east.
⛔ This page does not rule it and could not. It draws both readings, on the same triangle, so the question can be asked with a number attached. It is also not the only thing unstated up there: what a loft occupant can reach and whether fixed glazing changes the answer are 0.3a’s to say, and the fall-protection posture for operable openings is already an open PE item on the east wall (cover email §1.4).

Sliding the window EAST along the ruled stretch is free, and it is never worse. Hard against the ridge post the window leaves a 14.5 in stub that stops counting — Σb 66.5 in, util 0.476. Slid to the east end it leaves one uninterrupted 81 in segment at util 0.391. The generator sweeps every width from 0.57 in to the full stretch and asserts the east-most position never governs worse than the west-most one — it is a property of the geometry, not of one candidate. ⚠️ And it is not free of questions: the east jamb lands at the building corner, and no source details the corner framing or the hold-down anchorage there. Nothing is invented for it here.

A segment at h/b 3.474 is derated by the 4.3.4.2 Aspect Ratio Factor to 0.816, so it becomes the weakest link even though it adds length. Σb is a sum; utilisation is governed by a member. The generator asserts the inversion rather than asserting at it.

This page prices the pair — and it prices them three times, because on 2026-08-13 the PE-package review published a mechanism bracket in which this wall’s governing segment goes from 0.451 to 0.961 without a single opening being cut.

① The wall as ruled — and a sill that will not fit

At DATUM v9 a 2′×2′ window cannot sit above the kid-safe sill band. There are 20 inches up there, not 24. The plate underside is 62 and register 0.3a’s band starts at 42, so the rough opening available above it is 62 − 42 = 20 in. A 24 in tall opening on that sill would reach 66 — 4 in inside the top plate. So the owner’s square and the kid band are mutually exclusive by 4 inches, and that is exactly the tension the PE letter already puts on the table: “its sill is deliberately unset pending your read — our standing rule elevates operable glazing to 42 in for the kids, the egress function pulls the other way.” ⛔ This page does not resolve it. It measures it.

The two-window programme is hostage to a ruling nobody has made yet — unless the nailing rides with it. The one-window state survives the couple comfortably (0.736). Every two-window combination fails it. The 4 in edge nailing rescues exactly one of them — the narrow second window, 1.159 → 0.795 — and at 24 in it is not enough (1.009, over by 0.009). A capacity upgrade multiplies what is left; it cannot buy back a segment that has stopped counting.

What the three columns are, and what they are not

  • A — the 50/50 baseline. The N–S split the workbook publishes: two counted lines at the two edges of the diaphragm, half the base shear each (owner ruling R7). 675 lb ASD to this line.
    Basis: owner ruling R7, memo docs/decisions/2026-08-13-4x4-plate-and-nook-final.md §R7 · CALC: 9_TH_SW_E §I2 / §I3.
  • B — the §14.7 couple. Not a new analysis: the fourth of four mechanisms the workbook itself brackets for the E–W direction. Under it CHASE-SOUTH is unchanged and the residual E–W torsion is resolved as a couple into the N–S walls — 762 lb per line, which on this wall is larger than its entire direct share. ⚠ The E–W problem becomes an N–S problem, in the workbook’s own words. ⛔ No mechanism is adopted here. §14.7’s own banner says it: “THE MECHANISM IS A PE RULING, AND NOTHING HERE ADOPTS ONE”, over an open-front condition whose governing provisions are believed applicable and not transcribed.
    Basis: PE-package review docs/decisions/2026-08-13-pe-review-memo.md P1-1 · CALC: 2_LD_WIND §14.7 ‘THE E–W MECHANISM BRACKET’, row 4. Both cited because a utilisation printed on a page owes its rationale and its live calculation, not one of them.
  • C — tighter panel-edge nailing. The same Table 4.3A row at 4 in o.c. panel edges instead of the adopted 6 in: nominal wind unit shear 1065 plf against 730, a factor of 1.4589. It is on file precisely for this — 4_ENG_SW’s own note says the tighter rows were transcribed “so an instance that needs more capacity can move up the row without re-opening the standard”. It costs no Σb and no window.
    ⛔ What this page may NOT say about it. Table 4.3A’s tighter rows carry conditions — framing width at abutting panel edges, nail edge distance, panel layout — and those footnotes are not transcribed on 4_ENG_SW. Only the capacity numbers are. So the ratio is the table’s and the permissibility is not on file: tighter nailing is priced here as a capacity lever and is not adopted, not scheduled and not certified buildable at this framing. That is a research-and-PE item, and inventing the conditions would be exactly the failure the never-invent rule exists to stop.

⭐ What the combinations actually say

  • The budget on this wall is 16.39 in, and 18 in is already over it. Each segment the ruled window leaves is 35.25 in. A segment stops counting below h/3.5 = 18.86 in, so a second opening can take 35.25 − 18.86 = 16.39 in and no more. At 24 in the host segment leaves 11.25 in and stops counting entirely — one opening, one whole segment.
  • North or south is free, and that is worth knowing. E-1 and E-2 are mirror images and they are identical in every column — same Σb, same unit shear, same governing utilisation, to the last digit the generator can hold. Nothing on this wall is asymmetric. So the side is chosen on view, light, furniture and the ladder arrival, not on shear, and the generator asserts the equality rather than asserting at it.
  • The narrow second window is the only one that survives — and only with the nailing. E-3’s 16 in window leaves 19.25 in, which counts at h/b 3.429 but is derated hard (ARF 0.821). At the baseline it is comfortable (0.545); under the couple it fails (1.159); with the tighter nailing it passes (0.795).
  • Headers are cheap on this wall, and that is measured, not assumed. The ruled exit’s header runs at governing utilisation 0.181 — NOTCHED SHEAR @ combo 3 D+S. ⛔ That is evidence about this class of opening on this wall, not a header size for anything drawn here: no source states a header depth for these openings, so every rough opening runs to the plate’s underside with the header still to come out of it.
    Basis: register 1.2a-rev (R12/R13, 2026-08-13) · CALC: 9_TH_HDR_EXIT_E, GOVERNING UTILIZATION / §HDE1.

⚠ Where this arithmetic could be wrong, in either direction

In the wall’s favour — the engine is SEGMENTED-ONLY. 9_TH_SW_E’s SCOPE note: “SEGMENTED WALLS ONLY (SDPWS 4.3.5.1…). No perforated shear wall (4.3.5.3…) and no force-transfer-around-openings wall (4.3.5.2).” Both methods exist to credit sheathing above and below an opening — which is most of what a high band leaves behind. ⭐ So these prices are the conservative ones. But not by an amount anyone may assume, and choosing a method is a PE-and-workbook decision, not a study’s.

Against it — this line’s share is held FIXED while its Σb changes. The workbook’s SCOPE note says “NO SHEAR-WALL-LINE DISTRIBUTION (4.3.3.4)”, so every candidate here changes this wall’s Σb and nothing else. A real distribution would move force between EAST and WEST as one of them is opened, and which way depends on the diaphragm. Named so the assumption is visible.

And the couple column is not a ceiling. §14.7 brackets four mechanisms; the couple is the one that lands on this wall. Row 3 — two-support beam equilibrium, the row that satisfies moment equilibrium about a real point — puts CHASE-SOUTH at util 1.69 and drives SOUTH into reversal instead. The bracket is a band, not a worst case for every member at once.

  • An adopted nailing schedule, and any claim that the tighter Table 4.3A row’s framing and edge-distance conditions are met — they are not transcribed anywhere on file.

West-mid support — three ways to attach to the oak

⏸ Open. All three live; PE + arborist gated, supplier consult pending.
⛔ FROZEN at datum v7 · 2026-08-09 · not regenerated — it records what was known when the decision was made

STUDY — NOT PART OF THE DESIGN — ALL THREE ARE LIVE, NONE IS CHOSEN — PE + ARBORIST GATED — GENERATED FROM geometry.py

Three ways to hang the west beam off the oak

The west beam needs one intermediate support. The first choice was a sixth screw pile, and it is root-blocked — a large primary anchoring root we are not willing to cut. So the remaining three all touch the tree, and the question is what each one does to it.

What the tree is being asked to carry. The support takes 1,982 lb with the beam spliced (2,476 lb if it runs continuous), at a reach of 24.5 in from the trunk face. That reach turns the load into a 4,047 ft-lb twist, and a bracket cannot hold a twist at one point — it needs two attachments, one pulling out and one pushing in.

⭐ The single most useful number here

Spreading the two anchors further apart is free, and it is the whole game.
Anchors spacedLoad in EACH anchor
24″ apart2,000 lb 
36″ apart1,350 lb ⭐ a third less, for nothing but placing the bolts further apart

Both spacings are recovered from the published couple (M × 12 / P), not typed — if the published set ever stops closing, this study refuses to print a spacing nobody stated. Ask the supplier how much further the spacing can keep helping.

① CONFIG 1 — three-member right triangle, west face

OUR OWN PROPOSAL — NO SUPPLIER PRODUCT

Right angle at the TOP. Both tree bolts on one vertical member.

A vertical piece lies against the trunk with both tree connections on it, one at each end. An arm runs from its top out to the beam, and a diagonal closes the triangle back down to its foot. The diagonal pushes the lower bolt in; the arm pulls the upper bolt out — and pulling out is how a lag screw leaves a tree, which is why the upper anchor governs.

⛔ Do not confuse this with ② below. This one is apex-UP with the right angle at the top; the Tribeam is apex-DOWN. They have been mixed up before, in both directions. ⚠️ And this is the one option no product photo governs — it is our sketch, so a supplier must price and bless it rather than recognise it.

② CONFIG 2 — the Tribeam, south face, spanning both beams

SUPPLIER PRODUCT — DRAWN FROM THE PHOTOS ON FILE

Apex-DOWN: one long member across the top, two struts converging to a low anchor.

The biggest of the three, and the only one that touches both beams. A high tab carries a member across the top; two diagonals run down and inward to a single low anchor.

⛔ The trunk is not centred between the beams — 37″ to the west beam against 71.75″ to the east, nearly 2:1. A symmetric product on an asymmetric span is the open question, and it is the first thing to put to the supplier. ⚠️ No source publishes how this one splits its anchor loads, so this study says only what the geometry forces and leaves the spacing undimensioned rather than inventing one.

③ CONFIG 3 — knee-brace bracket

SUPPLIER PRODUCT — DRAWN FROM THE PHOTOS ON FILE

Arm at beam level; diagonal runs DOWN to a lower anchor.

The simplest. An arm bolts to the trunk at beam height and picks the beam up; a diagonal runs from the beam underside down to a second, lower trunk bolt. Because that diagonal is in compression — a prop, not a hanger — this option props the beam rather than hanging it, and the tree carries less than it does under ①.

The west nook — it is the west short-joist bay

The space between the west cabin wall and the oak has been carried as “the book nook” since the loft memo adopted it, with no dimension attached to it anywhere. It has one, and it is not a leftover: the nook is a floor framing bay, bounded by the west beam on one side and the west double header on the other.

1'-0"  wide, west beam CL to the west double header — and that is a bay, not a clearance.

The datum reaches the same 12.0 by two routes that are the same route: CUTOUT_HEADER_W_X = TRUNK_W_FACE_X 18 − TRUNK_STANDOFF 6, and SHORT_JOIST_SPAN_W, the span of the short joists that carry the floor there. The nook is that bay.

⭐ Width is RULED at 1 ft (owner, 2026-08-10). ⏸ Depth is open — the options are below, and this study does not pick one.

⭐ It is the part that has floor. The tree cutout — the hole with no floor in it — starts at X 12 and runs east to 60.5. Everything west of that line is deck: the west short-joist bay, 1'-0" of it, spanning from the west beam to the header. The nook is on the solid side of that boundary, which is exactly why it is usable at all.

⛔ Framed, not yet built. The four short joists J4–J7 (stations 54 · 64.5 · 75 · 85.5) and both headers are PLANNED — the as-built record says “no headers are hung; ran out of time”. And the west header carries its own open question: at 1'-0" of span against the east side’s 4'-0 1/4", “the west side is too short to need one” — delete or spec is OPEN (owner/PE). The LINE at X 12 is datum either way: it is where the cutout starts. Whether a member sits on it is not this study’s call.

Where the nook is, and what holds it up

North is up, east is right. Amber = the nook at its maximum depth. Hatched = the floor cutout, which has no floor. Tan = the oak. Heavy dark lines = the two cutout headers. Tan bands = the two double trimmers. Dashed grey = the short joists J4–J7, ⛔ not built.

A — CONTEXT PLAN. The headers frame into the trimmers; the trimmers sit 6" off the trunk’s N and S faces on both sides.

B — THE NOOK, ENLARGED. Width ruled; depth drawn as a band of options, none of them chosen.

How deep? — ⏸ not ruled

Depth is north–south, measured from the south chase wall on the S double trimmer, station 96, running north. North of wherever the nook wall lands, the space stays open, under the roof — the tree enclosure is a J, deliberately open north and northwest, and that openness is the reason the nook has a wall at all rather than simply petering out.

2'-2 1/4"  ⭐ MAXstation 69.75lands on the trunk’s west midline — the midpoint of the two double trimmers, which the datum carries as TRUNK_NS_CENTER_STATION. The owner: “in theory can run to w trunk midline but we don’t need that much.”
⚠ The max is a derived ceiling, not a proposal. The pocket is described in prose — “west of the trunk to the west beam wall, north to about the trunk’s N–S midpoint” — and geometry.py deliberately declines to encode its extents, saying so in terms: no source states them as dimensions, and inventing one there is exactly what that section exists to stop. What the datum does carry is the midpoint itself, TRUNK_NS_CENTER_STATION 69.75 — and it is a midpoint twice over, of the trunk’s own N/S edges and of the two double trimmers, because the 6" standoff is held on both sides. That is what makes 2'-2 1/4" computable at all.

What fits in 1'-0"

⭐ The binding constraint is the standoff, and it is worth seeing plainly. An 18 in shelf — the depth the plan’s “1'-6" to the trunk” looks like it offers — overruns the west header by 6". That 6" is the trunk standoff. A shelf built to it would run out past the header, over the cutout, and finish at the bark. There is the whole argument for a 1 ft width, in one line.
Why a sway envelope exists at all — the tree moves. An oak in wind is not a post. The trunk leans, sways and comes back, all day, every day, and it does it hardest in exactly the weather you would be inside the cabin. Anything standing in the space a living trunk sweeps through does not get grazed; it gets pushed, repeatedly, by a tree. The build guide is explicit that this is sway, not growth: at roughly an inch of radius a decade, growth would take about sixty years to matter — “the driver is TREE SWAY, which is a this-winter event and is still unquantified” (2.6a §2b/§12). ⚠ Nobody has measured how far this oak actually moves, and observing it in a wind is owed before the engineer’s visit.

⚠ But that allowance is an EAST-side figure, and it is not what sets this nook. TRUNK_SWAY_ALLOWANCE 12 exists to hold the ridge and the east chase wall off the trunk: its own source says the 12 in “sits INSIDE the chase (ridge west face = trunk east face + 12)”, and the single assertion in the datum that consumes it checks the east chase wall — 54.5 + 12 = 66.5, closing exactly. Nothing in the datum applies it westward.
⚠ Two clearances live in the datum, they are not the same number, and they apply to different sides. TRUNK_STANDOFF 6 is the framing standoff, field-verified, held on every side of the trunk — it is what sets the cutout, the headers, the trimmers, and therefore the nook. TRUNK_SWAY_ALLOWANCE 12 is the east-side figure for the chase. Reading the 12 westward is the mistake this geometry invites, because both numbers are about the same tree — but only one of them is drawn on this side of it. On the west side the boundary is a straight line: the west double header at X 12.

Six lines, four different jobs — and the one that looks most like “the front” carries the least

A cabin wall is never just a wall. It is some mix of carrying roof, resisting racking, holding glass and being a way out — and here those jobs land unevenly. The north wall, the one you walk up to, does none of the structural ones at all. Read this before the shear-wall decisions; they only make sense once you can see which line does what.
★★ And one of the lines is not a fixed length. The west wall runs to the nook wall — so how deep you make a storage nook decides whether EAST or WEST is the longest N–S shear candidate. An interiors decision moves a structural line. That is the second thing this page is for.

⏸ RULING STATE: OPEN — this study informs shear-wall selection, it does not make it.
The wall lines and lengths are measured and settled. Which walls get sheathed is not. That selection goes to the 4_ENG_SW engine and is decided on numbers that do not exist yet. There are six lines here, two of them E–W, and every one of them is a candidate. If anything here reads as a selection, it is being read wrong.

And the matrix below calls it BEARING — it stands on the west drop beam. A bearing wall that stops mid-span is not a thing. The west nook is the carve-out at the L’s west end and is why the south leg stops at X 12.0. Its width 12.0 in is ruled (it is the west short-joist bay, SHORT_JOIST_SPAN_W); its depth is open — the band is drawn to the stated maximum 26.25 in (station 69.75, the trunk’s west midline) with its north edge dashed, and the shallow option’s wall (station 84) dotted inside it. That is an envelope of the options, not a chosen line — and it is the figure that sets the west wall’s length.

2 · How long is each line — once you only count what is full height

Segmented shear sums full-height segments only. An opening does not weaken a wall a little; it removes its own width from that wall’s counted length (Σb). So the east wall’s ~30 in exit takes it from 94.5 in down to 64.5 in of counted line — a bite out of the bar, not a symbol on a plan.

⚠ And one bar is a range. The west wall’s length is 42 + the nook’s depth, and that depth is ⏸ not ruled — so WEST is drawn as a band from 54.0 in to 68.25 in, with the superseded 42.0 in figure struck where it used to end. No depth is picked here.

★★ It is a crossover, not a winner — and the thing that moves it is a storage decision. EAST counted is 64.5 in. WEST is 54.0 in at a 12 in nook, 64.5 in at 22.5 in — a dead tie — and 68.25 in at the 26.25 in maximum, where WEST is the longest N–S line in the building. The page used to claim a flat ratio here. There is no flat ratio; there is a 22.5 in crossover.
★★ An interiors storage decision moves a structural candidate line. How deep the book nook goes decides whether EAST or WEST is the longest N–S shear candidate. That makes the nook’s depth not a free interiors preference — it is the sharpest case in this project of a finish choice spending, or buying, structure. Whoever rules it has to be told. This is exactly what a wall study is for.
★ What survives from the old headline, and is stronger for being conditional: an opening still does not disqualify a wall. East holed stays competitive with west whole across the range — ahead of it below 22.5 in of nook, level at it, and within 5% of it even at the maximum. Picking the shorter line as the sole N–S shear wall because the longer one has a door in it would still have been the actual mistake. What is gone is the idea that the comparison has one fixed answer.

Σb is measured in the full-height wall — floor to plate, PLATE_Z 66 in (5'-6", LOCKED). Above that line the gable is a triangle that carries no roof: the ridge lands on its four posts, not on the gable wall. So a gable-peak opening still costs zero Σb — that finding is unchanged.

Ladder siting — the WEST edge, or the NORTH edge?

⭐ Ruled 2026-08-12: WEST is the default — the near-trunk arrival, the whole point of climbing up beside the oak. The tail taper (ruled the same day) lifts the landing to 4'-11 5/16"; NORTH stays documented as the alternative; a Year-3+ self-supported stair is reserved, not ruled out.

Where does the ladder land — the WEST edge, or the NORTH edge?

One climb, two places to put it. The difference is not taste: on the west you top out under the rafter tails, and on the north you top out under open sky. This page draws both to the datum and decides neither.

⭐ REVISED 2026-08-12 — OWNER RULING: EAVE TAILS TAPERED TO A 2.0 IN TIP (DATUM V8); THE PRE-TAPER V7 FIGURES ARE KEPT BELOW AS THE RECORD THE RULING WAS MADE AGAINST.

This page was drawn on datum v7 (2026-08-08c), the owner read it, and ruled the tails tapered on their underside to a 2 in tip — which is now datum v8 (2026-08-12). The ruling was made on the figures below, so those figures are kept, dated and labelled rather than overwritten: the west section draws the adopted cut solid and the superseded v7 soffit as a dashed ghost. ⚠ The siting question itself is UNCHANGED and still open. The taper moved one number on one side; it did not choose an edge.

⚠ This is not a licence to re-run a study. It is legitimate here for a narrow reason: the page had never been published, and the ruling it triggered is about the very geometry it draws. A study whose decision has landed is frozen — re-deriving it on a later datum destroys the record of what was known.

A north landing would supersede a standing ruling — also below. All of that is an owner call.

And 0.3 is the standing filter on all of it: kids up alone from age 4, permanent ladder, no lock. ⚠ No project source rules the ladder TYPE or its ANGLE, and this page does not set either.

⚠ Before anything else: the datum contradicts itself about where the ladder lands

Register row 0.4a, raised 2026-08-10, still OPEN. Twelve lines apart inside one comment block, geometry.py says both of these:
  • “The ladder lands in the unencased NW quadrant and you step north into the porch.” — a WEST-edge landing, in the zone between station 43.5 and the trunk’s N–S midpoint at station 69.75.
  • “the NW porch is where the ladder lands.” — the porch is NORTH of station 43.5, which is a different place.
The owner said 2026-08-10 “on outside of structure on ladder”, which narrows it but does not settle which edge. So “the standing plan” is not a single place, and this page draws the west reading as the west candidate rather than pretending the datum speaks with one voice. ⚠ When it is ruled, both lines get fixed in one commit — that is the discrepancy protocol, and it is not this page’s job.

① The plan — both candidates, and the roof over them

How to read it. The roof is drawn semi-transparent over everything, with its rafters at 16 in o.c. showing the rhythm only. The roof’s north edge is the gable line at station 16 — this design has no rake overhang (2.6a §3a.3), so north of that line there is nothing overhead at all. The west candidate is a zone, not a point: the NW pocket’s extents are prose in the datum and deliberately not encoded (geometry.py’s own TODO says so, in terms), so it is drawn between the two lines the prose does name. The north candidate is a zone for a different reason: no position along the rim has been chosen, and the headroom over the walk south changes with where you put it.
The ceiling gains 9.46 in for every foot you walk east. 66 in at the west wall line · 72 in at X 7.61 · 75.46 in at X 12 · capped at the ridge-beam soffit 107.635 in. That is register 0.4b’s rule, re-derived here from APEX_RISE / RIDGE_X — and it is exactly why where the ladder lands is a headroom question and not a preference.

② The two arrivals, at one vertical scale

⚠ The west collision, stated as arithmetic — and what the taper bought. The west deck edge sits 9.625 in outside the wall line (JOIST_OVERHANG_EW 5.625 + SIDE_RIM_W 4, closing on DECK_OVER_RIMS_EW 128), and the eave edge, 15 in NOMINAL past the wall line, reaches 5.375 in past the landing itself — so a climber on a rim-leaned ladder rises directly under the rafter tails, and that has not changed.

⭐ What changed is how much room is under them. The taper lifts the underside by the ledge’s share of the tip gain — (9.625 / 15) × 4.457 = 2.860 in over the landing, and the whole 4.457 in out at the eave edge:
  • over the landing: 56.44 → 59.30 in (4'-8 7/16" → 4'-11 5/16") — the upright-stature threshold at the moment of arrival
  • at the eave edge: 52.20 → 56.66 in
  • the duck: carrying register 0.4’s 72 in stature up the 4:1 line, the head now meets the cut tail at X -13.24 with the feet 14.5 in below deck level — it was 19.4 in, so the duck happens 4.9 in later up the climb (and 16.9 in on the slope-defining envelope, which is the figure register 0.4’s plane implies and the one this page led with at v7)
⚠ It is a real gain and it is not a fix. A 72 in adult still ducks 12.7 in at the landing (it was 15.6), still under the tails, still at the least stable instant of a climb that register 0.3 says will be made by a four-year-old, alone, sometimes in the dark.
⭐ The published plane, the real soffit, and the cut — three lines, and which one governs where. Every arrival figure in register 0.4 / 0.4b is measured on the datum’s slope-defining plane, which meets PLATE_Z exactly at the wall line. The rafter’s own soffit — geometry.py’s _soffit_w — passes through the birdsmouth seat, EAVE_SEAT_W 2.5 in inboard, and therefore sits 1.971 in lower everywhere. That correction is unchanged and still runs against the west option inside the room: a 72 in adult stands upright at X 10.11, not X 7.61, and the taper does not move that by a thousandth — datum v8 rule C keeps the cut wholly outboard of the bearings, so nothing indoors moves at all.

⚠ But OUTBOARD of the wall line the order of the lines now flips. Over the landing the cut tail sits at 59.30 against the envelope’s 58.41 — 0.889 in ABOVE the published plane, because the 2.860 in of taper outruns the 1.971 in correction. So register 0.4b’s 4'-10" is now conservative at the deck edge, where it used to be optimistic. ⚠ Only there. At the wall line and everywhere inside it, 0.4 and 0.4b still read high by 1.971 in.
⚠ The north price, and this page does not pay it. The north rim is the cantilever tip: 18 in NOMINAL past the post line, which is the PE cap (“18 exactly = the PE cap; if field asks >18, shift the rim south”), with the cross centreline 2 in inboard of that and the NE tip field-locked at 17.25. A ladder-head reaction at that tip is checked in no document on file — not in the calcs workbook, not in any memo. It is the same objection the 2026-07-04 memo raised against its own option B (“people congregating + any stair reaction at the tip is a live-load item”), and it has never been answered. This study states it and refuses to clear it. It is a question for the engineer, and it is the north option’s real cost.

⛔ What choosing NORTH actually costs in paperwork

D3 is a live ruling and a north landing overturns it. The 2026-08-03 memo adopted it flatly: “D3 — Ladder head lands SOUTH of the gable line. Free, layout-only, and it keeps the ladder→door path clear of anything at the gable plane. Adopted regardless of D1.” The memo is archived, and archived decisions still govern where they were not superseded — D3 was not.

⭐ But its stated reason was written for a door that no longer exists. D3’s justification is the ladder→door path, and in that memo the door was D2’s west-facing door on the N–S connector wall. D2 is DEMOTED — the owner adopted Option E on 2026-08-09 and the door is now north-facing at station 43.5, X 66.5–108. Whether D3’s reason survives the door move is exactly the owner question this page exists to put — and it is a question, not an answer: a rejection is only as durable as the fact under it, and reopening one is done with a new dated row, never by deleting the old one.

⚠ Three published figures this page could not reproduce

Drawing a thing to the datum is a check on the prose about it. These came out of that check. ⛔ NOTHING HAS BEEN CORRECTED IN ANY SOURCE FROM HERE — a study reports the arithmetic, the owner rules, and the owning document is fixed in its own commit. All three are raised, none is resolved.

1 · The west and east ledges look swapped in register 0.1b

The register’s “standing room” table gives WEST 10.4 in and EAST 9.6 in. Derived from the datum: the deck runs JOIST_OVERHANG_EW 5.625 + SIDE_RIM_W 4 = 9.625 in outside each beam centreline (and 108.75 + 2 × 9.625 = 128, the published over-rims width). The wall line and the west beam centreline are the same line in geometry.py’s own E–W frame, so the WEST ledge is 9.625; the 0.75 in of wall-versus-beam slop falls at the EAST, making that one 10.375. The register’s pair is the right pair with the sides exchanged. ⭐ It does not change this page’s argument — 9.625 is the west figure in either reading of the two E–W frames, and it makes the west arrival taller, not shorter.

2 · Register 0.4b’s “4'-10” at the west deck edge survives, but not by the route it was computed

On the derived 9.625 in ledge the envelope gives 58.412 in = 4'-10 7/16", which is 4'-10" to the nearest inch — the published figure. On the register’s 10.4 it is 57.821, which also rounds to 4'-10". The headline holds either way; the 0.75 in it was computed from does not.

3 · Register 0.4’s “a 6 ft adult clears at X 7.6” is an ENVELOPE figure

Against the datum’s slope-defining plane it reproduces exactly: 66 + 7.611 × 0.788321 = 72.00. Against the rafter’s actual soffit, which passes through the birdsmouth seat 2.5 in inboard, the same adult clears at X 10.111 — 2.5 in further into the room. Row 0.4 is marked DECIDED (geometry), so the difference is worth an owner’s eye. It is the same 1.971 in offset throughout, and it always runs the same way.

• And one thing that reconciles, stated so nobody re-derives it

NW_PORCH_DEPTH_NOMINAL is 47 in (“the deep (~47 in) NW porch”, D2 memo §1) while the as-built chain puts the north rim 43.5 in from the cabin’s north wall line. The difference is 3.5 in — exactly WALL_STUD_THK, which would follow if the ~47 were measured to the far face of that wall. ⚠ No source says that, the constant is NOMINAL and its memo is superseded on the layout; treat it as FIELD VERIFY, not as a resolution.

Sources, in priority order

1 · Building code / regulation. The drawn pitch is [REG] 29 CFR 1926.1053(b)(5)(i), which states it on the working length — “the horizontal distance from the top support to the foot … is approximately one-quarter of the working length”, i.e. 75.52° and a foot 21.43 in out. The trade rounds that to “4:1”, which is rise-to-run and gives 75.96° with the foot 20.75 in out — a difference of 0.68 in on the ground. ⚠ That is an OSHA construction-workplace rule, cited as the established practice for an illustrative angle. No project source rules a ladder angle, and this page does not set one. Separately: a ladder is not a code-compliant primary means of egress for habitable space (2026-07-04 §4) — an AHJ question, unanswered.
2 · Definitive sources — this project’s own decided record. geometry.py at DATUM v8 (2026-08-12) for every dimension; the 2026-07-04 access memo for the lean-to mounting, the solid-rim bearing, the grab rail and the A/B/C option table; the 2026-08-03 north-gable memo for D3; the 2026-08-09 porch-options study for Option E; the interiors register for 0.3 / 0.4 / 0.4a / 0.4b / 3.2.
3 · Trade practice. Not cited, and not needed — nothing on this page details a joint, a fixing or an assembly. When a ladder is actually specified, that is where its head fixing and its gate hardware will have to come from, after the two sources above.

Deliberately NOT drawn

  • A choice. Neither option is selected and no recommendation is made.
  • Any position along the north rim. The north candidate is a sliding zone; where it goes interacts with four guard posts whose stations no source states.
  • The ladder itself — type, width, rung spacing, tread form, material, how far the rails run above the landing, and how the head is fixed. The mounting is decided; nothing else about the ladder is, and the dashed outline is a study outline at an illustrative pitch with its arithmetic printed beside it.
  • The gate, its hardware, its hinge side and its swing. A self-closing, self-latching gate is ruled; nothing about it is specified, here or anywhere.
  • The grab rail beyond noting that it is ruled — no height, no length, no fixing.
  • Any structural clearance of the north cantilever tip under a ladder-head reaction. That is the one thing this page most wanted to settle and most refuses to. It goes to the engineer.
  • Any child stature figure. Register 0.3’s filter is stated in words. The 72 in figure on both sections is register 0.4’s own 6 ft adult, carried up the line as an illustration.
  • The NW pocket’s extents as dimensions. geometry.py refuses to encode them and so does this page.
  • The guard posts, on either edge — no source gives their E–W stations.
  • The roof’s finished outline, its fascia, soffit boards or drip edge. The sections draw the structural soffit plane; a finished soffit would sit at or below it, and would make the west case worse, never better.
  • The west-mid support. Open (S-104, PE + arborist), and its station is published in a frame this page does not convert.
  • Anything at all about stairs. The 2026-07-04 memo keeps a Year-3 stair on the table; that is a different question with a different footing.

Six walls, and each one can hold glass in a different way — or not at all

The plan study says what each wall is. This one asks what can go IN it: where a window can sit, how high its sill must be, which wall can be glass wholesale, and where a vent belongs. Everything is drawn to one common scale so the six can be read against each other — and the first thing that comparison shows is that they are not all the same height. The ceiling in this room is not flat, and two of the six walls are far taller than the rest.

★★ REVISED 2026-08-10, after owner review, before publication. The first draft of this page had two defects.
1 — it treated every wall as the same clear height. That figure is an eave-wall figure. geometry.py’s HEADROOM block (2.12 §9.2, ruled 2026-08-06) says it outright: “at the E/W eave walls the ceiling IS the plate line — the roof rises from there”. Corrected in §1, and the generator now refuses to write the eave figure as either interior wall’s clear height.
2 — it applied the kid-safe sill band to the fixed plexi panel — that is, to the very thing register 0.3 proposed as the remedy for breakable glass. Owner ruled the same day (register 0.3a): the band governs glazing that can OPEN or BREAK — glass and operable sash — and does not govern fixed plexi. Re-scoped throughout.
⏸ RULING STATE: OPEN — this study makes the window decisions DECIDABLE. It does not make them.
Register 1.2 (siting), 1.2c (the gable pair — 12 and 18 in are working figures), 1.3 / 1.3a / 1.3b (the plexi wall and its product) and 3.3a (venting) all remain open. 1.2a is decided — the second exit is on the EAST wall — but the egress-capable window’s siting is still open, and this page draws candidates, never a choice.

1 · The ceiling is not flat — and that governs everything below

The roof is a ridge-beam gable running north–south. So the ceiling over any east–west line rises from the plate at the west wall to the ridge, and falls again to the plate at the east wall. Two consequences the first draft missed:

  • At the eave walls the ceiling is the plate line — the roof rises away from them. Their height is the wall height, and nothing more.
  • Under the ridge, headroom is measured to the beam SOFFIT, Z_RIDGE_BOT 107.635 in, “because the 10 in ridge hangs into the space” (2.12 §9.2). It is not measured to Z_APEX (120 in), which is a seat-line construction point: nobody stands under it, and no view may print it as a head-height figure. This page obeys that literally, and its generator asserts it.
★ You arrive at the ladder with 66 in over your head, and you gain 9.46 in for every foot you walk east. A 6 ft adult is stooping at the west wall line and upright by X 7.6 — about eight inches in. That single number (0.7883 in per inch, the west plane’s own slope) explains every wall height on this page. Register row 0.4 records it.

3 · The six elevations, at one common scale

The three walls at a constant station run across the ridge, so a roof triangle stands above each of them; of the three at a constant X, two run under the eaves at constant plate height — and one does not. Each panel is plotted against the plan’s own axes (X increasing east; station increasing south), not oriented to a viewer, so the south gable reads exactly as it does in the plan study, east on the right.

How to read it. The pale blue band is the candidate glazing band — the 21 in between the 42 in kid-safe sill (solid red) and the underside of the top plate. It is a zone, not an opening: no window on this page has a width, a position or a head. The dashed red line at 34 in appears only on the two walls the owner named as egress candidates. Tan bands are the plate stack; tan diagonal hatch is solid wall; the dashed tan outline on the tall interior panel marks the trunk standing behind it, 36.5 in across and centred on that wall’s own midpoint. Amber crosshatch = the gable pair at the owner’s 18 in working width; green dotted = a vent zone, zone only.
⚠ The red hatched block on the east wall carries ONE dimension only: its ~30 in width, from register 1.2a. Its height is not ruled by anything, and it is shown sliding because its position in that wall is open too.
⚠ Four things the drawing says that a table would not.
1 — the two interior walls are drawn OPEN at the top, because the ceiling above them is known and their built height is not. One of them has a top that is a slope, not a line: it rises with the west plane and caps where it dies into the chase column’s head. Neither is shown as counted racking length.
2 — the NORTH gable has only ONE side. The wall runs X 66.5 → 108, and the ridge post occupies X 66.5 → 70.5 — so the post stands at this wall’s west end, not in the middle of it. A symmetric pair is not available here; the south gable is the only one where 1.2c’s pair can be symmetric.
3 — the east end of the interior E–W wall lands on the chase column, X 66.5, which datum v7 merged with the S-mid ridge post. That is the “frame attachment point” the owner named, and it is a real member.
4 — the tall interior wall’s ceiling is the ridge beam itself, drawn across the top of that panel. Its west face and the wall line are the same plane (CHASE_E_WALL_X = RIDGE_ARRIS_W), which is exactly why that wall gets the ridge’s height and the eave walls do not.

5 · Chase-east — the one wall that gets a product

Register 1.3a makes the chase east wall a plexi wall — it is the tree view. Register 1.3b names the product the owner found: OPTIX 0.118 in × 36 in × 72 in clear acrylic, ~$110, Lowe’s #11289. And §1 changed what this wall is: it stands at RIDGE_ARRIS_W, directly under the ridge beam, so the opening available is 52.5 in long × 106.1 in clear.

★★ That is a 52.5 × 106 in opening onto the trunk — 38.7 ft². The tree view, rather than a ribbon. The first draft drew this wall at the eave-wall height and made the plexi a clerestory strip. At its real height it is a nine-foot wall of glazing looking straight at the oak. The owner’s own instinct — one big upright sheet — is the right shape for it, and the arithmetic below says exactly how far one sheet gets.

★ The lead case: ONE sheet, 36 in along the wall × 72 in tall

Owner, 2026-08-10: one upright sheet “gives full view of trunk”, and side-by-side sheets “will be unsightly unless we frame the joint plus poses a weather barrier issue”. So on this page a seam is a cost, not a neutral option. Two things about that single sheet are worth stating exactly:

  • ★ “Full view of trunk” is literally true. The trunk is 36.5 in across (DERIVED — field verify) and its centreline sits at station 69.75, which is this wall’s own midpoint. A 36 in sheet centred on the wall is therefore centred on the tree, and shows 98.6% of its width.
  • ⚠ The height is not what it looks like. 72 in of a 106.1 in wall is 67.8%, not the ~80% assumed.
⚠ The two stated preferences cannot both hold, and this page does not choose between them.
★ “~80% of the chase height” is 84.9 in of glazing.
★ One seamless 72 in sheet gives 72 in.
→ a 72 in sheet is 12.9 in short of the 80% target. One sheet or 80% — not both. Buying the last 12.9 in costs a seam and at least one more sheet; the trade is drawn below, and it is the owner’s call, not this page’s.

★ “Perfectly frame the trunk” has an exact answer — and it is no

An equal margin on all four sides is impossible with this sheet, and it fails in two different directions:

  • At 36 in wide the side margin is 8.25 in each side. To get the same margin top and bottom, the sheet would have to be 89.64 in tall — taller than the 72 in it is.
  • At 72 in tall the margin is 17.07 in top and bottom. To match that at the sides, the opening would have to be only 18.36 in wide — narrower than the 36.5 in trunk, so it would stop being a full view of the tree at all.
★★ The resolution worth drawing: equal 8.25 in on LEFT, RIGHT and TOP, with the remaining 25.89 in solid BELOW. Three sides match and the fourth is deliberately different, which reads as a framed opening with a plinth rather than as a mistake — and the solid base is the part children and furniture actually hit. Its sill lands at 27.39 in. The centred alternative (17.07 top and bottom, 8.25 at the sides) is drawn beside it so the two can be compared. Neither is selected.

And the same wall, if it is only built to the plate line

Whether this wall is framed to the ceiling or stopped at the ordinary wall height is not stated by any source (§1). If it stops at the plate line, the sheet meets a much shorter opening, and these are the three cases — with option A now un-blocked, because the rule that used to rule it out was register 0.3’s kid-safe band, which 0.3a says does not govern fixed plexi:

A — one sheet laid long, sill at 27.0 in, 19.5 in trimmed off its length; it stands 36 in tall and 15 in of it sits below the 42 in line, which for a fixed plexi panel is now a description rather than a fault. A′ — the same sheet ripped to 21 in so it sits exactly in the band, worth doing only if the panel is ever glass or an operable sash, and it throws 15 in away. B — two stacked, 10.5 in trimmed, and one horizontal seam, which is now a cost.

⚠⚠ THE PANEL IS UNSIZED, AND THIS PAGE DOES NOT SIZE IT — and the taller it gets, the more that matters.
Whether 0.118 in acrylic may run this far without intermediate support is not established by anything on file. A 72 in tall unsupported acrylic panel is a bigger unverified question than the low ribbon the first draft drew, not a smaller one, and going to the full 106.1 in enlarges it again. Intermediate framing may well be required — that is unknown, and unknown is not a no.
Nor is it established whether a plastic panel in this location satisfies — or defeats — any safety-glazing requirement, nor how it behaves when a child runs into it. The opening is drawn; the panel is not. No figure for how far it may run, how much it deflects, or what it takes on impact appears anywhere on this page, and the generator refuses to write one.
⚠ The owner’s saved image (design-and-reference/plexi 2 sliding pane window.avif) is a marketing photo, not literature. It cannot close any of these. What can: the OPTIX / Plaskolite technical datasheet for 0.118 in clear acrylic.
⭐⭐ RULED 2026-08-10 — the trunk is NOT sealed to the roof (owner, verbatim: “we’re not sealing the trunk”; register R-1a). That is not a detail, it changes what this wall is. The chase is an open-air shaft: weather enters it by design. So CHASE-EAST is an EXTERIOR assembly, and the acrylic panel and its perimeter are the building envelope — this is a window onto open air, not an interior view onto a trunk.

⚠ Which raises the stakes on the unsized panel rather than settling them. It was an unverified structural span; it is now also the weather envelope of a wet shaft. Nothing on this page sizes it, claims it sheds water, or claims it does not.

⚠ Consequence to be designed, not a solved detail: rain and snow enter the shaft deliberately and drain down through the floor cutout, which is open around the trunk. No source states that path — it is stated here as a consequence of the ruling, and it needs designing.

⚠ Still OPEN — register R-1b: not sealing is not the same as no roof detail. The opening still needs its own geometry and an upstand or curb so water sheds INTO the shaft rather than back into the roof build-up. The owner’s working idea is to match the floor cutout — doubled trimmers and headers, on the rake. ⛔ Owner-HIL and a Fable datum pass; research-or-raise, never derived. Nothing is drawn for it here.

6 · The south gable — two equal rectangles, and where the area peaks

Register 1.2c: a symmetric pair about the S ridge post (X 66.5 → 70.5), not run to the eaves. The owner asked to see this as two equal rectangles at several widths rather than as the triangle above. Both rectangles are the same height, and that height is set by whichever slope runs out first — always the east one, because it is the steeper (53.82° against 38.25°) and its run to the wall line is only 37.5 in.

★★ The area of each rectangle PEAKS at 18.75 in wide — 25.63 in tall, 481 in² — and falls away on both sides. Past the peak, widening the pair loses more height than it gains width. So 24 in fits, and is a SMALLER window than 18 in (443 against 480 in²). The owner’s 18 in guess is within 0.2% of the best available — and 12 in gives up 13%. That is the whole answer to the question, and it is not a ruling: the widths are still a sweep.

The triangle drawn is the datum’s slope-defining construction, the same one the ceiling profile in §1 uses: it meets PLATE_Z at exactly 0.0000 at both wall lines, rising APEX_RISE 54 in over runs 68.5 and 39.5 to RIDGE_X. The point where the two rafter top planes intersect is a different construction and misses the plate at both ends; a figure taken off it has already been published wrong once, so this generator asserts the closure and refuses to name the other point.

7 · Gable vents — north and south

Register 3.3a: the roof is a single-skin cathedral with no attic and no roof cavity, so there is nothing above the ceiling to ventilate. What needs venting is the room, and the driver is not summer heat but condensation on the underside of the metal in cold weather. The gable peaks are then simply the room’s high vents, working on stack effect — which is the right instrument in the right place, and §1’s profile is why: the warm air goes to the ridge.

So a candidate vent zone is drawn at each gable peak, above the window rectangles — green dotted on the SOUTH and NORTH elevations. Two things about it are worth saying out loud:

  • ⚠ The peak is not one opening. The ridge post runs up through it to the ridge soffit, and the ridge beam sits end-on above that, so the zone is two slices on the south gable and one on the north.
  • South is sky; north is borrowed. The south gable at station 138 is a true exterior gable. The north wall at station 43.5 opens into the covered porch’s own roof volume, which is itself open to the north — a sheltered high vent with borrowed light, which register 1.2 read as a different and rather good property rather than a downgrade.
⚠ ZONE ONLY — no vent is sized on this page, and no sizing rule is quoted. How much ventilation this room needs is a code calculation and a building-science question, and no source for either is on file. Drawing a zone says where a vent belongs; it does not say how big it is. Register 3.3a is a research gate and it is still shut.

What would close the open items — sources, in priority order

1 · Building code / regulation. Whether a safety-glazing provision applies to a plastic panel in this location, and what it requires; whether the IRC emergency-escape provision applies to this structure at all (register 0.1 already flags this as an AHJ question, and its clear-opening figures as quoted-from-memory and unverified). Ask the AHJ; do not settle either from memory.
2 · Definitive sources — manufacturer and engineering. The OPTIX / Plaskolite technical datasheet for 0.118 in clear acrylic: its published support tables, its thermal movement figures and its fixing detail. That document, not a product page, is what makes the panel sizable — and at the heights §5 now draws, it is the single most valuable missing document on this page. The same class of source settles the single-skin condensation question in 3.3a.
3 · Trade practice. Only after the two above, and only for the fixing detail — how an acrylic panel is actually held in a timber frame so it can move.
⚠ The owner’s saved image is none of these three. It is a marketing photo of a product, and it was recorded as such the day it arrived.
⭐ One question that WAS on this list is now answered: whether this wall is inside or outside the weather line. It is outside — the trunk is not sealed (R-1a), so the chase is an open-air shaft. ⚠ What remains open is R-1b, the roof opening’s own geometry and its upstand.

Deliberately NOT drawn

  • Any window, at any size or position. Every glazed thing on this page is a zone or a candidate placement of a stated product. Register 1.2 is open; siting is exactly what it will decide.
  • Which wall gets the egress-capable window. The owner named the SOUTH and EAST walls as candidates; both are drawn with the lower sill line and neither is chosen. ⚠ That is a different question from the second exit, which register 1.2a decided (EAST) — and whose position within that wall is still open, so it is drawn sliding.
  • The built height of either interior wall — the ceiling above them is a datum fact and their own top is not, so both are drawn as open envelopes.
  • Header sizes, and any framing for any opening — jambs, sills, cripples, trimmers. None ruled, none drawn.
  • Stud counts, stud layout, nailing, hold-downs, sheathing type.
  • Any structural capacity claim for the acrylic panel — how far it may run without intermediate support, how much it deflects, how it takes an impact, and whether it is permitted where safety glazing is required. All UNSIZED; see §5.
  • Any weather-barrier detail or claim, for the panel, its perimeter or a seam. ⭐ This wall is now known to be outside the weather line (R-1a — the trunk is not sealed), which makes the detail more load-bearing, not less: the panel is the envelope. Nothing here details it, and R-1b — the roof opening and its upstand — is still open.
  • The drainage path out of the shaft. Water entering the open chase falls through the floor cutout, which is open around the trunk. That is a consequence of R-1a, stated so it is not forgotten — no source designs it, and nothing here sizes or details it.
  • Vent sizes, and any ventilation sizing rule. Zone only; see §7.
  • Shear-wall selection, and any counted racking length. Register 1.4 is reopened and handed to 4_ENG_SW. Every wall line on this page is a candidate; the 64.5 in figure quoted for the east wall is the plan study’s own candidate arithmetic, not a credit.
  • The west nook’s depth — register 2.2b is open, so the west wall is drawn as a range (54.0 to 68.25 in) and never as a number.
  • The north door’s leaf size. Register 3.2 is open and the roof does not force it; the door is drawn as a zone.
  • Blocking. That is register 2.1 and it has its own study — but note that every sill and head on this page will eventually want backing, and the bands were chosen before any of these openings were.
