STUDY — NOT PART OF THE DESIGN — A RECOMMENDATION, NOT A RULED SCHEDULE — HEIGHTS ARE OWNER JUDGEMENT, NOT A SOURCED STANDARD

Where does blocking go, when nobody knows yet what will hang on the walls?

Interiors register 2.1 · ⏸ OPEN — this page is the decision aid, and the decision is the owner’s. Wall carcass drawn from geometry.py at datum v7: plate line PLATE_Z 66 in (LOCKED), wall line WALL_SPAN 108 in, sole plate 1.5 in, doubled top plate 3.0 in → underside at 63 in, stud 1.5 × 3.5 dimensional at 16 in o.c. (register 1.1 + 1.1a-rev), clear bay 14.5 in.

⛔ The deadline arrives long before the decision feels urgent. Blocking is nearly free while a stud bay is open, and is demolition afterwards. The bays close when sheathing or interior finish goes on. So this has to be decided for things that will not be built for years — which is exactly the kind of item that gets deferred forever because nothing is pressing.

The proposal — bands, drawn against a child rather than against a wall

Three continuous heights on every wall. Two more are already there for free: the sole plate and the doubled top plate are continuous backing whether anyone plans for them or not. A fourth band is drawn as a candidate, visibly different, because that is the actual open question.

heightwhat it is forwhy that height
0″sole platealready there — free
16″bench seat, low shelfa small child’s seat height
34″desk, work surface, mid shelfa four-year-old works here
52″high shelf, hooks, picture railtop of a young child’s reach
~58–60″candidate fourth band deliberately above a young child’s reach
63″top plate underside (PLATE_Z 66 − 3) already there — free

⚠ The three heights are owner judgement (register 2.1), not a sourced standard. No anthropometric table is on file in this repo, so none is quoted here and the figure above is indicative only. Stating that is what makes the heights reviewable.

1 — Design for the occupant who was never told

This is the whole argument, and it is not really about carpentry. With bands, a future person hangs something anywhere along a line without knowing where the blocking is — because it is everywhere at that height. With points, they must have read a document. The building will outlive the document, and it will outlive the conversation that produced it.

Points also demand something impossible: that the entire interior be decided now. A shelf that moves eight inches has nothing behind it.

2 — The rule that actually sets the size

THE GOVERNING RULE “Blocking is not sized for the object. It is sized for a child hanging off it.”

A shelf holds books; the same shelf holds a child who decided it was a ladder rung. A hook holds a coat; it also gets used as a foothold. Foreseeable misuse is a design input, not user error.

⛔ And that is a sizing principle awaiting a real check — not a number this study may supply. Nothing in this repo states a shelf or blocking capacity, so no member size, no fastener and no pounds figure appears anywhere on this page. The bands above are drawn as lines for exactly that reason. Sizing is a structure-decisions §5 research gate.

3 — Write the heights into the building itself

Documents get lost. The structure does not. The band heights should be recorded on the building — marked inside a hatch, written on the framing before it is closed, or carried on the names plaque (register 3.15). That costs a pencil and it is the only part of this scheme that survives everyone who was in the room.

4 — The fourth band, and the question it actually raises

The fourth band earns its place only if you want a zone a small child cannot reach — in a room children use unsupervised from age 4 (register 0.3), somewhere to put things they should not get is a real safety instrument, not just storage.

⚠ But look at what the drawing shows. The top plate underside is already continuous backing at 63 in, free. A band at 58–60 sits only 3–5 in below it. So the real question is not “is an out-of-reach zone worth having” — it is whether 63 in is already high enough to be that zone, in which case the fourth band buys a few inches of convenience rather than a new capability. That is the owner’s call, and it is why the band is drawn as a candidate and not as a proposal.

5 — Beyond the bands: four things that are not band-shaped

Listed as open. ⛔ None is drawn as a detail — no ladder design, no grab-handle detail, no hinge specification appears in this study.

  • The loft ledger ends. The ledger lands on the south wall and hits every stud; the ends may want blocking. ⚠ And the drawing found a collision: the loft top is LOFT_TOP_Z 54 in with a frame member LOFT_FRAME_D 3 in deep, so the ledger zone is 51–54 in — and the 52 in band sits inside it. On that wall the two want the same height. Not resolved here; the ledger detail is not drawn.
  • Door hinges and any closer. Solid backing. Register 0.1 makes this life-safety, not preference: the door must open from the inside without a key, tool or special knowledge. A hinge screwed to nothing is that requirement failing quietly.
  • ⭐ A grab handle at the top of the ladder. Nobody had raised this. Permanent open ladder, no lock, unsupervised from age 4, arriving at deck level in the dark. It is the same class of item as the door, and the backing for it is free today.
  • Anything hung from the rafters — swing, hammock, hanging chair. ⛔ A different problem entirely, and it must not be folded into this one: that is a point load at mid-span on a dimensional 2×6 at 16 in o.c., not a wall-blocking question. It goes to the engine, not to a band.

What this study deliberately does NOT draw

omittedwhy
Any blocking member size, species, fastener or nailing ⛔ No source in this repo states one. Bands are drawn as lines.
Any capacity — pounds, per-band or per-hook ⛔ Nothing in this repo states a shelf or blocking capacity. The “child hanging off it” rule is a sizing principle awaiting a real check.
Any reach or anthropometric standard ⛔ No table is on file. The heights are owner judgement; the figure is indicative and labelled so on the drawing.
The ladder, the grab handle, the door hinges/closer Named as open items above. Detailing any of them here would be inventing.
The loft ledger itself, and its end condition Its zone is shown because the arithmetic collides with the 52 band. The connection is unstated by any source.
Any shear or diaphragm claim for the blocking Walls are 66 in, so a 4×8 panel runs vertically with no horizontal seam — there is no panel-edge blocking to coordinate with, and no claim is made either way.
Bands on a specific wall schedule The proposal is every wall. Which walls are sheathed is register 1.4, reopened and handed to 4_ENG_SW.
Two facts about the wall that the bands have to live with. The last bay on this wall is 9.0 in clear, not 14.5 — 108 does not divide by 16. And the west nook is 6 in usable of an 18 in space (register 2.2a): the trunk’s 12 in sway envelope takes the rest, and ⛔ nothing may be blocked, shelved or hung into that envelope — it is a tree strike, not a clearance.

STUDY — NOT PART OF THE DESIGN — THE 5'-6" LOCK STANDS, NOTHING HERE IS ADOPTED — GENERATED FROM geometry.py, NOT HAND-DRAWN

What would a 6'-0" wall buy the WEST ladder arrival — and what would it cost?

A what-if, asked the day the tails were tapered. The taper bought 2.86 in at the west landing and it is ruled. Wall height is the other lever, and it is inside the owner’s own ruled band — so this page draws what 6 more inches would look like, and what they would drag with them.

⛔ THE 5'-6" LOCK STANDS. This page adopts nothing. PLATE_Z = 66 is an owner lock of 2026-08-07 (2.6a §8, the kid-scale rebase) and it governs until an owner rules otherwise. Every figure here at plate 72 is a what-if: it is not a datum value, it exists only inside this page, and no sheet, workbook or memo may be measured against it.
⭐ But 6'-0" is INSIDE the band the owner already ruled. The 2026-08-07 lock’s own words, as 2.6a §8 carries them: “7' is out on the jumping concern; 5–6' is in, 5.5 as compromise”. So 72 in is not a reopening of a closed question — it is a re-choice within a band that is still open at its top end. ⚠ Mechanically it is still a real move: a PLATE_Z datum pass (Fable-only under the model policy), the workbook mirrors that quote the plate, and a full re-render of the construction set. This study does none of that and asks for none of it.

① The arrival, at 66 and at 72

How to read it. Both panels are at one vertical scale and both draw the adopted v8 tapered tail solid — the cut is ruled, so it is not drawn as an option in either. The only difference between the two panels is the plate: 2.6a §8 states that a taller wall leaves “pitch, rafter cuts, roof area, snow and the 9'-0" span all identical — the roof simply translates up”, and the generator asserts exactly that (the arrival must gain precisely 6 in, or the construction is refused).
At the west landing: 59.30 in as ruled today → 65.30 in at a 72 plate. 4'-11 5/16" → 5'-5 5/16". A 72 in adult’s duck at the deck edge goes 12.7 in → 6.7 in — a real improvement, and still a duck. The tails still overhang the landing by 5.375 in; wall height does not touch that.

② ⭐ The question underneath: why must loft headroom move with the wall?

It must not. That is the finding. LOFT_TOP_Z = 54 is an owner CHOICE, not a structural constraint — 2.12 §2b, in terms: “The loft height above the cabin floor had never been set anywhere in the project… Owner decision: 54 inches, chosen to favour the space below.” The loft is a net in a ledger frame whose edges are the three walls and the front beam (2.12 §2); the ledger ties into the S-wall stud run and can sit anywhere in it. Nothing in any source on file pins its elevation to the wall height.

So “walls +6” and “loft +6” are two independent knobs, and the jumping objection that produced the 5'-6" lock is an objection to one particular setting of them — not to wall height as such.

What can the EAST wall hold, now that it has slack?

On 2026-08-13 the owner ruled the WEST wall built — full height, sheathed, no openings. That made the north–south direction a two-line system, and the east wall’s governing segment fell from 0.903 to 0.451. It now has margin for openings it could not afford the day before. This page prices that margin.

⛔ NOTHING ON THIS PAGE IS SELECTED. Register 1.2 — the window schedule — is OPEN. The only ruled opening on this wall is 1.2a’s second exit (~30 in, EAST, 2026-08-10, PE-confirm), and even its station is not ruled: 1.2a states two layouts and picks neither. Everything else here is a dashed candidate with its arithmetic beside it.
⭐ The premise, quoted rather than claimed. 9_TH_SW_E’s own live headline, post-1f025d2: “LIVE -- EAST at the TWO-LINE split (R7): governing segment util 0.451 at v 125.6 plf, hold-down T 671 lb -- down from 0.903 / 251.1 plf / 1,362 lb when this was the only counted N-S line. WEST now carries the other half (9_TH_SW_W, util 0.357). The one remaining candidate, CHASE-EAST, would take the governing segment to 0.314 -- and it is the ruled plexi wall, so that stays priced-not-proposed.”

Basis: owner ruling R7, memo docs/decisions/2026-08-13-4x4-plate-and-nook-final.md §R7 · CALC: 9_TH_SW_E §I2 ‘THE OPENING POSITION IS A LIVE VARIABLE’ and §I3 ‘THE N–S CANDIDATE LINES’. Both cited because a utilisation printed on a page owes its rationale and its live calculation, not one of them.

① The wall as it stands

How to read it. The east wall is an eave wall, so register 1.5a rules that “the ceiling IS the plate line” — the roof rises away from it, westward. ⭐ That is the single most important fact on this page and it is a constraint: there is no gable triangle above this wall, so the free opening the S and N gables have (register 1.2, “gable-peak openings cost ZERO Σb”) does not exist here. A “clerestory” on the east wall means a high band inside the shear wall, just under the plate — and it is not free.
A high clerestory light costs exactly what a door costs: its own width. The segmented method (SDPWS 4.3.5.1, and 9_TH_SW_E’s SCOPE note says so in terms) counts only full-height segments — floor to top plate, no opening. A 24 in light 42 in up the wall breaks that segment as completely as a 24 in door does. The glass is cheap; the Σb is not.

⚠ Where this arithmetic could be wrong in the wall’s favour

The engine is SEGMENTED-ONLY, and it says so. 9_TH_SW_E’s SCOPE note: “SEGMENTED WALLS ONLY (SDPWS 4.3.5.1…). No perforated shear wall (4.3.5.3…) and no force-transfer-around-openings wall (4.3.5.2).” Both of those methods exist precisely to credit the sheathing above and below an opening, which is most of what a high clerestory leaves behind. ⭐ So the prices on this page are the conservative ones, and a clerestory could be cheaper than it looks here — but not by an amount anyone may assume. Choosing a method is an engineering decision with its own conditions and its own detailing; it is a PE and workbook question, and a study does not make it. It is named here so the conservatism is visible rather than silent.

⚠ And one that could run the other way: this wall’s share of the N–S shear is held FIXED. Under ruling R7 the two N–S lines each carry half, and the workbook’s SCOPE note says in terms: “NO SHEAR-WALL-LINE DISTRIBUTION (4.3.3.4) — V arrives at C4 already assigned to this line.” So every candidate on this page changes this wall’s Σb and nothing else. A real distribution would move force between the lines as one of them is opened — which direction it moves depends on the diaphragm and is not ours to assume. Named so the assumption is visible.

  • Any header depth — unsourced for these openings (register 0.3’s own reconciliation), so every rough opening runs to the plate underside and the header comes out of it later.
  • Any glazing product, sash type, operation, hardware or glass specification. Register 1.3 (the plexi barrier) is parked, 1.3b’s product gate is open, and none of it is decided here.
  • Any code-compliance verdict. The SDPWS numbers are the workbook’s transcription and the utilisations are ours, not a licensed engineer’s.
  • New wind arithmetic of any kind — including the utilisation at a 72 in plate.
  • A perforated or force-transfer-around-openings treatment. Named above, not run.
  • Hold-down hardware. The tensions the workbook reports are demands; no device is selected anywhere in this project, which is why 9_TH_SW_E’s deflection is flagged NOT QUOTABLE and is not quoted here.
  • Venting. Register 3.3a is a shut research gate; a clerestory that opens is a vent, and that is exactly why it is not sized here.

STUDY — NOT PART OF THE DESIGN — THE EGRESS WINDOW IS A RULED REQUIREMENT AND ITS SIZE IS NOT — NO OPENING SIZE IS ADOPTED — GENERATED FROM geometry.py AND A RECALCULATED calcs.xlsx

The SOUTH wall — above and below the loft, and the egress window

One wall, cut in two by the loft, with opposite economics on either side of the top plate. Above it the gable triangle is not part of the shear wall at all, so an opening up there is free. Below it is the shear wall itself — and that is where the owner has ruled a window.

⭐ RULED 2026-08-13 (owner), register 1.2f: ONE window in the SOUTH wall OPPOSITE THE NORTH DOOR (door X 66.5–108), sized for emergency exit, in the below-loft zone, exiting onto the 6 in south ledge.

⛔ What is ruled is the REQUIREMENT. The SIZE and the POSITION are OPEN, and this page adopts neither. Register 0.1b rules that egress sizing here is “a research gate, not the code figure by default” — so the reference figures below are marked [REG] REFERENCE, NOT ADOPTED and nothing on this page selects a window.
⭐ Why the window is affordable at all, quoted rather than claimed. 9_TH_SW_S’s own live headline, post-1f025d2: “LIVE -- TWO-LINE E-W STATE (owner ruling R10): SOUTH carries HALF the E-W base shear at v 97.4 plf of 332.2 plf allowable, util 0.293, h/b 0.61, hold-down T 430 lb -- down from util 0.587 / T 966 lb when it was the only counted E-W line. CHASE-SOUTH carries the other half: util 0.581 at v 193.1 plf, T 1,671 lb (9_TH_SW_CS). *** WHAT THE SECOND LINE BOUGHT IS UNIT-SHEAR RELIEF AND REDUNDANCY, NOT TORSION: the two E-W lines sit on the SAME side of the load line, so E-W torsion falls only 23.1% (2_LD_WIND 14.4), against 94 % in N-S where EAST and WEST straddle it.”

Basis: owner ruling R10, memo docs/decisions/2026-08-13-4x4-plate-and-nook-final.md §R10 · CALC: 9_TH_SW_S §I2 (the CHASE-SOUTH candidate row, now superseded by the ruling) and its RESULT block. Both cited because a printed utilisation owes its rationale and its live calculation.

① The wall, floor to apex

Above the top plate an opening is free. Below it, it costs its own width. Shear walls are the full-height segments floor → top plate; the rake wall above is a separate element. So the gable triangle (54 in of it) costs zero Σb — and the 12 in strip between the loft top and the plate does not: it is still shear wall, and an opening there is priced exactly like one below the loft.

② The free half — the gable pair

This half is effectively settled, and it was settled by arithmetic. Register 1.2c rules the shape (two equal rectangles flanking the S ridge post, X 66.5–70.5 — not run to the eaves, not the triangle above) and 1.2d ruled the arithmetic: the area of each rectangle peaks at w = 18.75 in, h 25.63, 481 in² each, because area = w × tan θE × (37.5 − w) and that maximises at half the east run. ⭐ 24 in fits and is a SMALLER window than 18 in.

⚠️ Two true statements that look like a contradiction, reconciled: register 1.2d says the owner’s 18 in guess is “within 4%” of optimal and the 2026-08-10 wall-elevations study says “within 0.2%”. Both are right and they measure different things — 18 is 4% off the peak by WIDTH and 0.2% off it by AREA. The curve is flat at its top, which is the useful fact: the width choice barely matters, so choose it for looks, framing or venting.

The door-wall extension: what it buys, and how much trunk it hides

The cabin's north wall line is the last wall lever the E–W direction has. Extending it west adds shear length on the far side of the wind resultant — and puts sheathing between you and the oak. This page prices both sides of that trade and chooses neither.

THE OWNER'S ASK, VERBATIM — 2026-08-13 “need to see studies of these options to visualize before decision is made; want tree trunk exposed experience while on porch but a portion can be concealed by wall extension if it buys structural integrity.”
The wall tops out at the plate (66 in). The oak carries on to the roof soffit — 92.6 in above the deck at its centre-line. Everything you keep is in that gap. And the gap is smaller than it sounds, because the oak stands only 8 in behind the wall: from mid-porch at a 60 in eye, the maximum extension leaves 27% of the visible trunk face showing. The shorter one leaves 44%.

⏸ Ruling state — nothing here is selected

The owner deferred this decision in order to see it drawn. Three extension lengths are on the page as candidates: none, a 24.5 in segment to X 42, and a 42.5 in segment to X 24. None is recommended here, and this page recommends nothing. The register rows it informs — 1.4 (which walls are sheathed) and 1.2 (the window schedule, since a port in this segment is a variant) — stay open. A ruling on it is an owner call, and the arithmetic then belongs to calcs.xlsx, not here.

The setup, in three facts

  • The wall line. Station 43.5 — the N double trimmer. The cabin's north wall runs X 66.5–108 today and carries the north-facing door. West of X 66.5 there is no wall and no header: the roof spans on over the covered porch, and that open slot is the tree view.
  • The load line. Station 77.0 — the centroid of the E–W loaded face, which runs station 16 to 138 because the roof carries north over the porch even though no cabin wall does (calcs.xlsx · 2_LD_WIND section 11e, name wind__load_cx_ew). Both counted E–W walls — SOUTH at 138 and CHASE-SOUTH at 96 — sit south of it, by 61 in and 19 in. Nothing counted sits north of it.
  • The oak. X 18–54.5, stations 51.5–88, ∅36.5 in derived — FIELD VERIFY at deck height. Its north face stands 8 inches south of the wall line, not eight feet.
⚠️ FALSIFIED WHILE DRAWING — 1 of 3. The task brief described the oak as “8+ ft south of the wall line” and asked for the cutoff to be derived at “8.35 ft behind”. The datum says TRUNK_N_EDGE_STATION 51.5 against TRIMMER_N_STATION 43.5 — 8 inches, a factor of twelve. The generator refuses to build if that ever exceeds a foot, because the whole sight geometry turns on it: at eight feet a low eye would see over the wall easily; at eight inches it barely sees past it at all. ⛔ Nothing has been corrected in any source from here.

Figure 1 — the plan: what the extension covers

Three standing positions, each with the two rays that graze the oak. Where those rays cross the wall line is the oak's shadow on it — and a wall matters only where it overlaps that shadow.

⭐ The finding the plan produces on its own. From P2, by the door, the oak's shadow runs X 52.8–77.4 — entirely east of X 42. So for that standpoint, option C costs exactly what option B costs (both 72% at the reference eye) while buying 16.9% more torsion reduction. The extra 18 in of wall is free from the door. It is not free from mid-porch, and it is not free from the north edge. That is asserted in the generator, not read off the picture.

The passage is load-bearing on the ruling, and it is the softest number here. Memo R6 (docs/decisions/2026-08-13-4x4-plate-and-nook-final.md) sizes a 24 in NOMINAL ladder allowance — but it states that 24 as a N–S landing depth (band = 52.5 − nook depth, stations 43.5 → 69.75 = 26.25 in at the ruled depth). Reading it as an E–W clear width at the trimmer line, which is what bounds option C, is a transfer to a different axis. ⛔ No source on file states a passage width. It is drawn NOMINAL and FIELD VERIFY, and if it grows, option C shortens inch for inch. (Falsification 2 of 3.)

Figure 2 — the money view: looking south from the porch

Why the oak is drawn where it is

The wall lives in the plane of station 43.5. So the honest way to draw what it hides is to project the oak onto that plane from the eye, and then ask a flat question: which of the projected oak falls inside the rectangle the wall occupies? For a point on the trunk at station s, with the eye at station sv and height h:

t = (43.5 − sv) / (s − sv)    Xproj = xv + t(x − xv)    Zproj = h + t(z − h)

Two consequences fall straight out, and both are asserted in the generator. ⭐ Along any one sightline the apparent height of the oak does not depend on the eye at all — only its position does; it is exactly t × the oak's own visible height. On the ray to the trunk's north face from mid-porch, t = 0.6322, so 92.6 in of real trunk appears as 58.5 in — whether a child or an adult is looking. ⭐ And an eye exactly at the plate cuts the oak at the plate, from any distance — below it the sightline rises and you lose more; above it the line falls and you lose less. The plate height is the hinge of the whole question.

Figure 3 — the similar triangle, drawn

The closed form the section draws: Zcut = eye + (PLATE − eye) × (s − sv) / (43.5 − sv). At mid-porch (station 29.75) the distance ratio to the oak's north face is 1.5818, so a 60 in eye is cut at 69.49 in = 5'-9 1/2" and a 72 in one at 62.51 in = 5'-2 1/2". Step back to the porch's north edge (station 16) and the ratio falls to 1.2909: the same 60 in eye is cut at 67.75 in instead. Backing away recovers trunk; walking up to the wall loses it.

It is arithmetically impossible, because station 43.5 is only 33.5 in north of the resultant while SOUTH is 61 in south of it with 9 ft of length pulling. ⚠️ Read what “torsion” means in this workbook before spending anything on it. 2_LD_WIND section 11 declares a flexible-diaphragm tributary distribution and states the consequence in terms: a flexible diaphragm does not distribute torsion at all, so the eccentricity computed in section 11e is not resisted by anything on that tab — it is REPORTED. So these figures are a planning-level measure of plan asymmetry, not a checked demand on anything. A rigid analysis is unavailable, because it needs a diaphragm stiffness that is not established. Reducing the number is still worth something — a better-centred plan is a better-centred plan — but nothing on this page clears a load path, and a licensed PE rules on all of it.

The honest secondary notes

The segment's own arithmetic

  • Aspect. Counted to the plate, option B is h/b 2.694 and option C is 1.553. Both sit inside the blocked wood-structural-panel limit of 3.5 that 4_ENG_SW's CODE BASIS block transcribes from SDPWS Table 4.3.4 — but only C clears the h/b 2.0 threshold at which SDPWS 4.3.4.2's Aspect Ratio Factor begins cutting capacity. B takes a factor of 0.913; C takes 1.000. Computed with the identical construction the workbook uses — verified by reproducing 9_TH_SW_CS's own published ARF (1.000 at aspect 1.9750) before printing anything.
  • Counted to the plate, not to the sloped ceiling. CHASE-SOUTH is counted to its full sloped ceiling (section 14.3); this page counts the extension to the plate, and says so. That reading is favourable on both currencies at once — a shorter wall has the better aspect ratio and hides less oak — which is exactly why it should be stated rather than assumed. Building it taller is a different option and a different page.
  • Where it bears. On the N double trimmer, the same doubled member the floor frames into — not on a beam. 2_LD_WIND section 14.6 flags the identical substrate question for CHASE-SOUTH's hold-downs at the S trimmer, and names it an unruled application for the PE. This one would be the same class of question at the other end of the cutout. Nothing here checks it.
  • It is dry-ish, not dry. The segment lives under the covered porch, on its north face weather-exposed. That is an assembly question (R-1a's exterior-class treatment for CHASE-SOUTH is the precedent), not a geometry one, and it is not priced here.

What else the same wall would do

  • It is the NW wind baffle the 2026-07-04 memo wished for. That memo calls NW “the site's hard corner” and asks for “a small wind baffle / half-jamb to knock down the worst drive-in while staying open”. An extension along the trimmer is exactly that — and note the memo's own words: small, and staying open. Option C is not small.
  • A port toward the oak is a real variant, and it is not drawn. An opening in the extension trades sightline back for Σb: any hole removes its own width from the counted length, and the segment is short enough that the aspect ratio of what remains is the binding worry, not the hole. ⛔ No port is sized, positioned, priced or drawn on this page — that is register 1.2's and 4_ENG_SW's work, and it needs the segmented-method layout the east wall got, not a sketch.
  • The alternative nobody has authored. The only documented way to stiffen this corner without a wall is the 2026-07-04 memo's “1 knee brace each way at the exposed NW post” — and that memo says in terms it is “belt-and-suspenders, not a portal frame”. ⛔ No document in this project designs, sizes or checks a porch portal frame, and none is drawn or dimensioned here. It is named as an engineering-hours item and left there.
⚠️ A standing document disagrees with the live workbook, and it is worth a dated look. The 2026-07-04 memo argued the NW notch was structurally comfortable partly because “~6 ft of N wall and ~6 ft of W wall” remain “intact as shear panels”. The live workbook rules the NORTH line STRUCTURALLY FREE with length 0 and counts nothing from it (2_LD_WIND section 11b, the six-wall table; no wall dead is charged for it either). The workbook is the later and more explicit statement, so it governs — but the memo's lateral argument rests on a premise the workbook has since withdrawn, and that is a fact the owner should have in hand when reading either. ⛔ Neither document was edited from here.

Deliberately NOT drawn

  • A recommendation. The owner deferred this to see it; presenting the trade is the whole job.
  • A portal frame — no member, no brace, no geometry, no capacity.
  • A port — no size, no position, no price, no header.
  • Any new wind arithmetic. Adding a third counted E–W line changes the tributary split and therefore the per-line demand on 9_TH_SW_S and 9_TH_SW_CS. That is calcs.xlsx's work and it is not done here; the V/Σb column is a direction-average comparison metric, not any line's design v.
  • Any child stature or eye height, and no glazing, plexi or ladder detail.
  • The door — register 3.2 is open and no leaf is sized here.
  • Anything east of X 66.5. The door wall exists; this page does not re-open it.

What this page would need in order to be decided

  • An owner ruling on how much of the oak the porch may lose — the table above is the currency, and it is a taste question, not an engineering one. Until it is made, every length here stays a candidate.
  • A ruled passage width at the trimmer line, since option C's length is set by it and no source states one. FIELD VERIFY at ladder procurement.
  • A calcs task if any length is adopted: Σb, a 9_TH_SW_* instance for the segment, hold-downs at both ends on the trimmer, the tributary re-split, and the torsion re-rank — the same bundle R7 and R10 each triggered.

What is actually at the four corners of the top plate?

R27 closed the doubled-plate question on the ground that “the corner tie is hardware under every candidate”. That is right — and it makes the next question unavoidable, because the tie of record ties the plate to a member that is no longer primary. This page walks the plate ring corner by corner, from the sources, and draws what it finds. Three of the four corners have no scheduled tie and two have no stated member to tie to.

① The plate ring, and the six joints in it

Every perpendicular member at Z 66 on file is 4 in wide — R21’s door-wall plate, the eave plates themselves, and (until R29 retired it) the C/H header. Which is why the tie geometry in Figures 3 and 4 can be drawn honestly while the member’s identity stays unstated. The landing is 4 in whatever the answer turns out to be — and R29 makes that answer overdue rather than merely open, because the retired scheme was the only one that ever named a member here.

Two live sources, one corner post, and the reason one of them gave has evaporated.

⭐⭐ R29 turned this from a disagreement into an ORPHAN. The solid 4×4 was adopted 2026-08-05b as part of the C/H stack (“one width through the whole gable stack”), and the checklist’s stated reason is the strap schedule — J1–J4, every one of them a C/H joint. Retiring C/H retires the reason, and what is left standing is the 2026-07-22 built-up-corner decision and the general wall-framing basis. On a built-up 3-stud corner at 4.5 in the v9 plate steps 0.25 in per side — the same quarter inch datum v9 rule C declares dissolved, reappearing with its sign reversed (post wider than plate, not narrower). ⭐ And R28’s half-lap wants the solid 4×4: a 4-in plate laps flush over a true 4×4; over a 4.5-in built-up it leaves a half-inch step and seats the lap on a layered top. ⛔ OPEN — owner ruling owed. This page draws neither as resolved.

④ ⭐ The corner detail, as R28 ruled it

⭐ R28 (owner, 2026-08-14) — the FORM is ruled, the SPEC is not. Three options were put up: (a) run-through + butt with a flat steel tie, (b) half-lap over the corner post, (c) 45° miter.
optionstatuswhy it matters here
(b) HALF-LAP over the post ⭐ LEAD — owner, R28 Each plate keeps a 2-in tongue; interlocked; the joint bears fully on the post; pinned through the lap into the post.
(a) BUTT + HTP37Z ALTERNATE — owner, R28 Owner-specified part. 3″×7″ Heavy Tie Plate, ZMAX, flat on the top face across the joint.
belt-and-suspenders
vertical corner straps		 ⭐ PROPOSED — owner, R28 follow-on One flat strap on each outer corner face, post face up across the outside of the lapped plates. 2 per corner, 8 total. Completes the corner as an uplift node and backs the lap pin. ⛔ Part not final — MSTA12Z-class candidate, registry check + PE.
(c) 45° MITER ⛔ OUT — owner, R28 Kept as a struck row only, per the register’s nothing-is-deleted rule.
⛔ R28 rules the form. It does not schedule a joint, size a pin, or state a capacity — and neither does this page.
The lap square is the post’s own footprint, and the eave plate must take the upper tongue. 4×4 in, because POST_W = PLATE_W = 4. And the handedness is derived, not chosen: the rafter birdsmouth seats on the plate top within 2.5 in of the outer face — inside that square. A lower-tongue eave plate would remove the seat at exactly the corner the end rafter lands on. The generator refuses to print the argument if that ever stops being true.
⛔ Three things the half-lap carries that a steel tie does not.
  1. It removes 50 % of each member at the corner (2 of 4 in). The plate-notching provision this project could find is R602.6.1, which addresses cuts for piping and ductwork and calls for a tie above 50 %. Nothing on file states whether it reaches a structural half-lap, and this page does not decide it. PE / AHJ.
  2. It is not a tie listed in Table R602.3.2. R602.3.2’s exception permits the single plate where tied per that table. A lap is not on it. So the half-lap on its own leaves the prescriptive path and becomes an engineered alternative under R104.11 — the alternate (a) stays on it.
  3. ⭐ They are not mutually exclusive. Because the eave plate takes the upper tongue, the corner’s top face is continuous — so a flat plate can ride over a lapped corner. Whether both are wanted is the PE’s call; the geometry does not forbid it.
⛔ The pin is the one thing no source states. The owner asked for it from established practice or manufacturer literature. What is on file: nothing describing a pin for a half-lapped top plate. What can be said without inventing is geometry — the lap is 4 in of wood, so a screw of length L leaves L − 4 in the post, and this project’s own SDWS22800DB (8 in Strong-Drive SDWS TIMBER, IAPMO-UES ER-192) leaves exactly 4 in. ⛔ It is named as a candidate on length alone. No count, no edge distance, no capacity, no pattern. And the registry rule bites: SDWS22800DB is APPROVED at guard-post-base and nowhere else — this is a new application and needs its own dated row. PE TO SPECIFY.

⑤ The HTP37Z, from the manufacturer’s own table

⭐ Definitive data — transcribed verbatim from Simpson Strong-Tie Wood Construction Connectors catalogue C-C-CAN2022 p.285, 'Strap Ties (cont.)' table, HTP37Z row. ⚠ That is the Canadian catalogue and its numbers are factored resistances to CSA O86-14 (LSD), not ASD allowable loads; KD is the CSA duration-of-load factor. The US allowable-load row is NOT on file anywhere in this repo, and the ESR on file (ESR-2105) does not cover the HTP family — checked.
propertypublished valuenote
gauge16 ga = 0.065 in in ZMAX (G185), or 0.06 in uncoated — catalogue p.24, US Standard Steel Gauge Equivalents
dimensionsW 3 × L 7 in 3.5 in each side of a centred joint
fasteners (total)(20) 10d x 1 1/2" (0.148" dia. x 1 1/2" long) 10 per member — catalogue note 2: “Use half of the nails in each member being connected to achieve the listed resistances.” (the same half-the-fasteners rule ESR-2105 imposes on the MSTA straps, and the rule that killed the MSTA24 at J1)
factored resistance
D.Fir–L		 1,610 lb (KD 1.00) · 1,850 lb (KD 1.15) ⛔ LSD, not ASD. These are not comparable to the 285.7 lb ASD collector demand, and this page does not compare them. Mixing strength and ASD bases has already produced one false alarm on this project.
factored resistance
S-P-F		 1,270 lb (KD 1.00) · 1,460 lb (KD 1.15)
What CAN be said, and it is what R28 said: the HTP37Z exceeds the prescriptive minimum — in steel and in size. 0.065 in against Table R602.3.2’s 0.036 in is 1.81×; 7 in against 6 in is 1.17×. ⭐ And the code’s 0.036 in is 20-gauge uncoated steel on Simpson’s own equivalents table — so the comparison is like for like, and it is a steel comparison, not a load one. No basis conversion is needed to make it, which is exactly why this page makes it and makes no other.

⑥ Why the tie had to be re-chosen at all

The prescriptive code plate fits the member. The scheduled strap does not. Option (i)’s 3-in leg lands inside 4 in with 1 in to spare. Option (ii) is scheduled 7 fasteners over 9 in per member and there are only 4 in of member — roughly 3–4 holes at the NOMINAL pitch. ⚠ FIELD VERIFY: STRAP_HOLE_PITCH_NOMINAL is a declared range, not a published pitch, and 2.6a’s own standing rule is to lay the real strap against the real member before ordering.
⛔ What this page does NOT do with that. It does not state an allowable for a reduced fastener count. ESR-2105’s 1,315 lb is a listed value for the listed fastening; converting a hole count into a capacity is a PE call under R104.11, and doing the division here would be exactly the kind of authoritative-looking guess the never-invent rule exists to stop. What the page states is a count, which is geometry.

⑦ The code panel — 2021 IRC R602.3.2

⚠ Transcribed, not read from an original. No IRC page is on file in this repo. Everything in this panel comes from docs/decisions/2026-08-14-top-plate-corner-question.md §1, which consolidates a sourced code-research pass. the exceptionwhat it requiresthis building
R602.3.2 Exception A single top plate is permitted where the plate is tied at joints, corners, intersections and in-line splices per Table R602.3.2. ⭐ The construction R5/R27 ruled is prescriptively sanctioned — it is not an engineered departure.
Table R602.3.2
SDC A/B row		 3″ × 6″ × 0.036″ galvanised plate, (6) 8d box nails each side, at corners and intersections. The site is SDC A/B. A Simpson TP37 matches the spec — but see the registry warning below.
in-line splices 12″ plate, 12 nails. ⭐ Moot. Each 122-in run is one 12-ft stick, zero splices — which is also why the zero-splice premise must survive any change at T2.
condition 2 Rafters/joists centred over studs within 1 in. The design stack-frames. ⚠ A standing requirement, forever, not a one-time check — it is the discipline a single plate buys its simplicity with.
condition 3 The plate may be omitted over headers where the header is “adequately tied to adjacent wall sections in accordance with Table R602.3.2”. ⭐ This is the code’s own answer to the C/H gable header: a steel tie, never a lap — which is precisely where 2.6a §6.5 landed independently in 2026-08-05b.
jurisdiction The state UCC enforces the 2021 IRC for new permit applications since 2026-07-01. ⚠ the local AHJ edition is confirmed at the memo’s level of research only; the J10 entry records that an edition question has bitten this project before.
⛔ THE COMPONENT-REGISTRY TRAP, NAMED. The TP37 is already on this project — two of them, tying the Year-1 west drop-beam splice (3.125×7 in, 20 ga, 32 holes; 1.6_drop_beams.md). That approval is for that application and does not transfer here. A component may be approved in one application and rejected in another — and the TP37 is not in docs/components/ at all (8 of ~18 seeded), so its absence means not yet seeded, never no ruling exists. Two things travel with it that a corner would have to answer: (a) coating — the TP37 is G90 only, there is no ZMAX SKU, against a project coating rule of ZMAX + HDG/SD on green wet-service stock; (b) fasteners — its listed fastening is 0.131×1½ nails or #9×1½ screws, while Table R602.3.2 calls for 8d box nails. Those are not the same fastener, and nothing on file reconciles them.

The proposed top-plate ring, drawn on the datum

Four single rough true 4×4 sticks at Z 66, closing a ring around the station 16–138 envelope: the two eave plates that already exist, plus a new plate on each gable line. Six solid posts carry it, two of which frame the west ladder entry. The owner asked to “visualize or more detail” before ruling. Here is the ring as the sources actually place it — including the two-inch registration clash it walks into at every single post, which no source has had to answer before because no member has ever been asked to land on a gable line.

⑤ One detail, up to six joints

The side-framed plate end is the ring’s single biggest ask — and it is not new. Because the ridge posts run continuous, a plate meeting one cannot bear on top of it: the end grain frames into the post’s face. R21’s door-wall plate already has that condition at both of its ends, and raise 7 names the connector as unruled. The ring adds four more instances of the same detail. ⭐ That is a cleaner PE ask than six one-offs: one detail to rule, up to six places to use it.

⑥ ⭐ The two-inch question — what does a station mean?

The ring is the first thing this project has built that has to land on a gable line, and the two documents that place things there do not mean the same thing by “station 16”. The interiors register states wall extents — a wall “runs sta 16 → 43.5”, i.e. those numbers are faces. The as-built chain states member centrelines — geometry.py asserts station 16 is “to the cross CL”. They differ by exactly half a member: 2 in.
Why the page draws the wall-extent reading. It is the only one that keeps both ruled figures intact: R5’s eave plate stays one uncut 10'-2" stick, and register 0.4a’s ladder landing band stays 2'-2 1/4". The centreline reading grows the eave stick to 10'-6", pushes the ring 2 in past the roof’s own edge at both gable lines, and — the one that bites — leaves the west entry 1'-10 1/4" clear, below the owner’s 24-in NOMINAL ladder allowance, spending the 2¼ in of spare that 2.2b’s max-depth ruling was careful to preserve. ⚠ FIELD VERIFY applies to that allowance either way — it is NOMINAL until the ladder is bought.
⛔ OPEN — and it is one ruling, not four. The same 2 in shows up at every ring post:
  • the gable plate’s end gets 2 in of face against the ridge post instead of 4 — half the contact R21’s ends get;
  • corner posts 1, 2, 3 and 5 get 2 in of the doubled 2×8 nailer / 4×10 cross under them instead of 4;
  • post 4 gets 2 in of the N double trimmer (band 41.5→45.5, from TRIM_PLY_HALF_W);
  • and the west entry either keeps 2'-2 1/4" or drops to 1'-10 1/4".
⚠ The nailer’s own N–S registration is stated by no source at all — NAILER_D 8 is its depth; its 4-in width is derived from MEMBERS['nailer'] (“doubled 2×8 … rough true-2”). The offsets above are computed off the two members whose registration is in the datum: the cross and the ridge post. Owner ruling owed, then a Fable datum pass to write it down.

The north gable triangle: open, screened, or sheathed

The triangle above the ring plate at station 16 — the roof’s own north edge, over the open porch face. Three options, the framing identical in all three, and one check that decides whether “open is free” or whether open re-prices the uplift chain. That check turns out to hinge on which of two north walls you are talking about, which is why this page begins by separating them.

③ ⭐⭐ THE DECIDING CHECK — ASCE 7-16 §26.2 enclosure classification

What the workbook actually carries today

No classification at all — deliberately. 2_LD_WIND row 182 states the convention in terms: “ENCLOSURE IS A PER-CONSUMER BINDING, NOT A TAB-LEVEL SETTING. No cell reads ‘the’ enclosure class — every consumer names which state it reads. There is deliberately NO single wind__gcpi name: the two states below are BOTH live, every design-pressure row below computes BOTH.” Both GCpi values are live cells — ±0.18 enclosed and ±0.55 partially enclosed, ASCE 7-16 Table 26.13-1. Consumers that adopt one say so on their own row: the pile/uplift chain adopts ENCLOSED (9_TH_PILE_C F7, 2_LD_TAKEDOWN §5 — “that is the adopted classification… THE PARTIALLY-ENCLOSED ALTERNATES EXIST AND ARE NAMED”). The tab’s own note on GCpi calls it “the biggest single demand lever” and hands the classification to PE/AHJ.

What the lever is worth, priced from the tab’s own two columns (no re-derivation — both columns are live and were recalculated today):

Basis for all of it: V = 115 mph ult, Exposure C adopted, qh = 25.00 psf [2_LD_WIND §V3.0 velocity-pressure ladder, C181]. The partially-enclosed column is not decoration — the whole uplift and hold-down chain would re-run on it.

The test, worked on both live readings

ASCE 7-16 §26.2 makes a building partially enclosed only if all three hold: (1) Ao > 1.1 Aoi · (2) Ao > the lesser of 4 sf and 0.01 Ag · (3) Aoi/Agi ≤ 0.20. Condition (2) clears by more than 15× on every row below (Ag = 49.5 + 20.25 = 69.75 sf → threshold 0.698 sf) and is guarded as a non-issue; condition (3) is bounded well under 0.20 by any plausible envelope area. Condition (1) — the dominant-opening test — is the only one that is ever close, and it is the one worked here, for wind on the north face, which is the governing direction for this question.

READING 1 — the envelope CLOSES at station 43.5 (the porch bay is outside it)

The covered porch is roofed but open on three faces (north, east and west); on this reading it is an open-sided extension and the cabin’s envelope is the door wall at station 43.5. ⭐ The station-16 triangle then appears in no term of the test — not Ao, not Aoi, not Ag, not Agi. Options (a), (b) and (c) give identical arithmetic, and open is free.

The margin in row 1b is 0.043 sf on a 12.43 sf threshold. ⛔ No source states whether that triangle is open or filled. The proposals memo §1 details “both gable lines” — stations 16 and 138 — and is silent on 43.5.

On this reading the windward wall for north wind is the porch’s open north face at station 16 — which is where this study’s triangle lives. The station-43.5 door becomes an interior opening and drops out of the envelope; the porch’s two side faces (11.84 sf each) become envelope openings and enter Aoi, which is what makes the threshold high enough to matter.

Under reading 2 the same triangle straddles condition (1): sheathed, Ao = 41.33 sf against a 59.07 sf threshold and the building is not partially enclosed; open or screened, Ao = 61.58 sf and it is — a 4.3% overshoot, carried entirely by the 20.25 sf of triangle. That is GCpi 0.18 → 0.55, i.e. +48% on per-post roof uplift and +46% on net corner uplift. ⛔ Which reading governs is the PE’s call and no source on file makes it.
⭐ A consequence worth stating plainly, because the memo does not make this argument. P2 recommends sheathing on boundary robustness, cavity closure and appearance. The stronger argument for (c) is the one above: sheathing removes 20.25 sf from the windward face’s opening on the one reading where the classification is live, and that classification is the workbook’s own “biggest single demand lever”. Symmetrically, (b) SCREENED buys nothing here: insect screen resists no pressure and closes no opening under §26.2, so (b) is (a) for enclosure purposes. ⛔ This is an observation about the arithmetic, not a selection — the owner rules.

④ The other four issues, worked

② Roof-diaphragm boundary — P10 lands in all three options

Confirmed from 2.6a §6.6, which pre-dates the memo and rules the members outright: “Blocking — Solid 2× between rafters, above the beam — and at the eave line, both planes,” placed there explicitly because “the 7/16 ZIP roof is element ③ of §6.5, and panel edges need a member to nail to at the boundaries.” That covers the ridge and eave boundaries. The gable-line boundary is P1’s raked cap — and the memo itself says the cap is retained in the open and screened variants, “the diaphragm boundary and the rake need the members regardless.”

⭐ So the boundary MEMBER and its nailing edge are present in all three options, and the memo’s “boundary robustness” argument for sheathing is weaker than it reads. ⚠ But it does not vanish, and this page will not overstate it: what sheathing adds is a braced panel behind the boundary member, and the memo’s own (b-2) carries the exact residual as a PE item — “the roof-diaphragm boundary then rides the raked cap + end-rafter blocking alone, without a sheathed panel bracing it: PE to confirm boundary adequacy in that configuration.” The argument narrows from “you need a boundary” to “you need the boundary braced”, and only the PE closes it.

⚠ Note the top boundary here is the sheathing plane, not an end-rafter soffit: 2.6a re-struck the rafter layout in 2026-08-06 so that no rafter falls in a gable-wall plane (owner constraint: both gable walls must die into the ceiling), insetting the end rafter from each gable line. The raked cap is therefore the only member on the gable line, in every option.

③ Weather — what comes through, and where it lands

Wind-driven rain and blowing snow enter high, through 20.25 sf of triangle at the north end, and fall into a covered porch that is 2'-3 1/2" deep (station 16 → 43.5). That is a narrow bay — the landing zone is the porch deck and the face of the R21 door wall, including the door itself. The triangle’s lowest point is at the eaves and its apex is at the ridge soffit (9'-10" above the floor), so anything driven through it has the whole porch depth to fall across and very little roof to fall under. ⛔ This is a lifestyle call, not a structural one, and the page does not weigh it — but it is the one issue on this list where the 2'-3 1/2" number does the deciding.

④ Critters and birds — why (b) exists

An open triangle against a ridge is the classic nesting geometry: sheltered, high, dry at the apex, invisible from the deck, and directly connected to the cold-roof cavity above the furring. Option (b) is exactly the answer to this and nothing else — it closes the aperture to wildlife while leaving it open to air, light and view. ⭐ Its cost is that it buys nothing on any of the other four issues: screen is not a diaphragm panel, not an opening closure under §26.2, and not a weather barrier.

⑤ What the workbook charges either way — and a second erratum

Wind sail: charged in full, regardless. 2_LD_WIND §1f derives the gable face from geometry as T1 (wall rectangle 49.5 sf) + T2 (triangle 20.25 sf) + the two rake/eave slivers = 71.434 sf, centroid 4.008 ft above deck, and that is “THE OVERTURNING FACE (§3 C20)”. The triangle is in it as solid area. So an open or screened triangle leaves the sail charge conservative — the model charges area that is not there. Nothing needs changing for (a) or (b); (c) simply makes the model true.

Triangle dead: ~143.775 lb, and today it is charged nowhere on the north. At dead2__wall_psf = 7.1 psf [2_LD_DEAD §6], 20.25 sf × 7.1 psf = 143.775 lb — the figure 2_LD_DEAD C78 already carries for the south triangle. On the north, C53 reads 0. Under (a) or (b) that zero stays right (there is no skin to weigh) and the charge is moot; under (c) a real figure is owed.

  • The proposals memo §1.2 says adopting the sheathed north triangle “makes that row real”, citing 2_LD_DEAD C53. Three dated corrections owed — Domain B for the cells, Domain C for the memo’s cite. ⛔ Nothing was changed here.

⑤ ⭐ VERDICT PANEL — what would make each option defensible

(a) OPEN — the owner’s preference — is defensible as-preferred if, and only if, all three of these hold:
  1. The PE reads the envelope as closing at station 43.5 (reading 1), so the station-16 triangle is outside it and cannot enter §26.2. This is the reading the workbook’s own wall inventory already implies — 2_LD_WIND row 369: “North of it is the covered porch, which the roof spans but no cabin wall encloses” — but it is implied, never ruled.
  2. P10 lands, so the gable-line boundary member (the raked cap) exists regardless — which 2.6a §6.6 already rules for the ridge and eave lines and P1 supplies at the gable — and the PE confirms boundary adequacy with the cap unbraced by a panel, which is the memo’s own (b-2) residual.
  3. The weather and wildlife consequences are accepted as lifestyle costs on a 2'-3 1/2" porch — or bought off with (b), which answers the wildlife half at no structural cost and no enclosure benefit.

⛔ What would FORCE (c) SHEATHED: the PE reading the covered porch bay as part of the envelope (reading 2). On that reading the open triangle is what carries Ao across 1.1 Aoi — 41.33 sf fails, 61.58 sf passes — and the building classifies partially enclosed, GCpi 0.55. The whole uplift chain then re-runs at +48% per-post roof uplift, +46% net corner uplift and +29% on stud C&C suction — and the pile, hold-down and clip checks that currently bind the ENCLOSED column all move with it. On that reading (c) is not a preference, it is the cheap way out.

What would force neither: a PE ruling that the classification is partially enclosed anyway — because the porch face below Z 66 is 41.33 sf of permanent opening that R32 already ruled open, and no choice about the triangle can close it. If that is the answer, the triangle reverts to a weather-and-wildlife question and the owner’s preference stands on its own merits.

The four post-base conditions

Ten posts stand on this deck — four ridge posts and six ring posts — and they do not land the same way. This page draws all four base conditions side by side, on the datum, with the demand and the seat arithmetic each one actually carries.

⭐⭐ THE OWNER’S QUESTION, CONFIRMED — AND SHARPENED.

Yes: the six ring posts and the four ridge posts have different base conditions. But the dividing line is not “ridge vs ring”, and the four ridge posts are not alike either. The real distinction is whether the member is CONTINUOUS through the floor plane or STARTS on it:

  • The four ridge posts are continuous. RIDGE_POST_FLOOR_TO_SOFFIT = 8'-11 5/8" holds at all four stations (2.6a, datum v6 rule D) — each is one stick from its bearing chain to the ridge soffit. A continuous member cannot stand on a bottom plate, so there is no bottom plate anywhere in conditions ① and ②.
  • The six ring posts start on the floor. P7 proposes they land ON the 1½-in PT bottom plate, which is exactly why the ruled cut is 5'-0 1/2" — plate underside 62 less the bottom plate 1.5 (R33-A).
  • And the ridge posts split again, because what is under the floor at a gable station (a doubled 2×8 nailer on the Year-1 cross) is not what is under it at a mid station (a double trimmer that must be bypassed). Different chain, ~7× the demand.

Four conditions, then — and a fifth would exist if post 6 were counted separately from the other five ring posts, which is how this page treats it, because its bearing is the one that is FIELD-PENDING.

② The four conditions, side by side

⛔ These are STACK DIAGRAMS, not dimensioned sections. Member depths are the datum’s own (NAILER_D 8, CROSS_D 10, JOIST_D 8, DROP_BEAM_D 10). The below-floor seat elevations are stated by no source — that is precisely what J12 asks the PE for — so none is drawn, and a build guard refuses the page if any Z value appears below the floor line.

③ Condition ① — RIDGE POST at a GABLE station (16 / 138)

Chain: the continuous ridge post bears directly on the doubled 2×8 gable nailer → a scribed shim pack → the Year-1 flush 4×10 cross. ⛔ No bottom plate.

  • Why a shim at all — it is already required, before this proposal. The nailer’s own arithmetic demands it: 0.985 utilisation gap-open on the no-cull basis, falling to 0.333 shimmed [LIVING memo §13]. P5 only details a shim the structure already needed.
  • What P5 proposes: a shim pack of exterior-grade structural plywood, plies HORIZONTAL (load through the panel thickness), full nailer-width × full 4-in post footprint minimum, field-scribed to the computed crown gap; galvanized steel plate as the equal alternate at thin gaps. The rule stated so it cannot be built wrong: no end-grain shim, no tapered softwood-shingle pairs under a structural seat.
  • ⛔ The shim MATERIAL is open, and the memo says so. §7: “no code provision and no manufacturer/engineering literature found that names a shim material for a wood post-bearing seat” — nearest kin is FEMA P-804’s “compression blocks”. The geometry is proposed firmly; the material is tier-3 trade practice and the PE rules. This page draws no thickness for it, and a guard enforces that.
  • The tie: two flat vertical straps per post, post face → nailer face, fasteners clustered within ~3–4 in of the joint line (the 2.6a §6.4 green-shrinkage rule). ⛔ No part is named on the drawing — the memo proposes an MSTA12Z-class strap, and the component registry forbids inferring a ruling across applications: MSTA12Z’s only registry application is J4, which is gated on the now-RETIRED C/H scheme. A NEW dated application row is owed, PE TO CONFIRM.

④ Condition ② — RIDGE POST at a MID station (43.5 / 96)

Chain: the continuous ridge post → full-depth squash blocking flanking the double trimmer on BOTH sides → direct to the NEW 4×10 cross. ⛔ No bottom plate, same reason as ①.

  • ⭐ The trimmer is BYPASSED, not loaded. The load may not enter the trimmer in bending [LIVING §11] — the blocking takes it straight past to the cross. The two-sided fit also avoids the one-sided prying mode the guard-base history documents.
  • Reused, not invented: this is the same detail already installed under the ridge posts (set 7d / Cabin r82).
  • Both mid posts are MERGED members and their heads are PACKED TIGHT (owner ruling 2026-08-08 — 2.12 §11d reversed): S mid is the chase column (datum v7 rule A, one member two jobs); N mid is the door-wall west post (datum v10 rule D). So the base seat is where all vertical adjustment lives — there is no head gap to take it up. That is what makes condition ② the demanding one.
  • ⚠ What rides on this seat: the §10.3 differential-shrinkage stack turns on the per-station cross-grain height, which turns on this detail — a named PE question carried on J12 since datum v6. This proposal puts a concrete detail under it; it does not answer it.

Demands [MEMO 2026-08-15 proposals §2 · CALC: calcs.xlsx 9_TH_RIDGE_3SPAN §5]. Seat arithmetic [CALC: '9_TH_POST_RIDGE' §BEARING PERP (rows 43–55)]: bearing area 16 in² (the full 4×4 footprint), Fc⊥′ green = 555 × CM 0.67 × Cb 1.09375 = 406.71 psi (NDS Supp. Table 4A wet service, no exception taken) → allowable 6,507 lb per seat. Worst station 0.148. Both seats of every post (cross below, ridge soffit above) are numerically identical — same area, species, derate and load. Slenderness le/d = 16.5 ≤ 50 (NDS 3.7.1.4, PASS); governing axial utilisation 0.0935, so bearing governs the member, not buckling.

⑤ Condition ③ — RING / JAMB POST (six posts)

Chain: a 5'-0 1/2" solid rough 4×4 standing ON the 1½-in PT bottom plate, on the subfloor, over full-depth squash blocking in the bay below, down to its own bearing chain.

  • ⭐ The bottom plate is why the cut is 5'-0 1/2" — plate underside 62 less the 1½-in bottom plate (R33-A, the same figure as the ruled stud pre-cut). Under the alternate (plate-interrupted) the post would be 62 instead. P7 proposes post-on-plate, and keeps the plate continuous past the post: one wall-assembly detail everywhere, continuous sill seal, continuous shear-wall bottom-plate nailing, no notched plate ends to detail.
  • Why the bearing is not a problem: P7 states it at a bounding 1,500 lb corner reaction — fc⊥ ≈ 94 psi against a deliberately pessimistic wet floor of 372 psi (555 × CM 0.67, the green Eastern Hemlock–Tamarack basis; any PT southern pine plate is denser) → ≈ 0.25 utilisation. ⚠ That is the memo’s bounding figure, not a computed reaction — no ring post has a computed demand anywhere (see the open items).
  • ⭐ R34 — registration. The corner posts centre on the as-built NAILER lines, never the N–S crosses or the E–W beams, which are not square. The owner, from the field: “in order for cabin to square the posts need to be centered on double nailers.” The datum corroborates: the N cross fans 0.644° off the rim square, so a square line on it is flush at the east end and 1.22 in proud at the west (NAILER_N_STRAY_W_DERIVED). Tape precision remains FIELD-PENDING — FIELD VERIFY — but nothing is blocked on it.
  • Post 4 is the exception among the five: it lands on the N double trimmer at the 1.2e wall’s south end (R31), not on a nailer.
  • The tie: two flat vertical straps per post, one per available outer face, post face → rim/nailer/trimmer face, clustered at the joint line. At the four plate corners these sit below the R28 belt-and-suspenders corner straps (post top → plate) — same family, same face, one detail language top and bottom.
  • ⭐ The absence of a formed post base was RESEARCHED, not assumed (§3.2): Simpson’s formed caps/bases are U-saddles made to surfaced 3½-in widths and a true-4.0 rough post will not seat; the FPBB44 is a fence-retrofit part (wrong finish, wrong substrate); AWC DCA 6 publishes no flat-strap post attachment and its post-to-beam family does not fit a flat true-4 base on a deck. So the strap pair rests on the tension-strap family precedent — legitimate precisely because gravity stays wood-to-wood bearing and the straps carry tension only. The PE confirms an assembly, not a SKU.

⑥ Condition ④ — POST 6, the special case (station 69.75)

Everything in condition ③, except what is under the blocking.

⛔ POST 6 IS THE ONE BASE WITH A REAL GAP, NOT JUST AN OPEN TAG.
  • Its footprint is 69.75 → 73.75, which falls in the bay between joists J5 (64.5) and J6 (75) — no joist lands under it. That is the entire reason it needs its own condition, and it is asserted in the build: the drawn footprint and the computed footprint must both fall inside the bay or the page refuses to build.
  • P7 proposes full-depth squash blocking in that bay, post → block → the west DROP beam line — the ridge posts’ own installed detail (set 7d / Cabin r82) reused, not invented.
  • ⚠ The as-driven west beam position under the footprint is FIELD-PENDING (v10 rule G). The beam is tilted as driven.
  • ⚠ And the beam’s own nearest support going south is itself NOMINAL: the planned Year-2 west-mid TAB, 14.45 in away, root-blocked at probe, PE + arborist gated. ⭐ Frame warning, guarded here: W_YR2_MID_STATION_PLANNED_NOMINAL = 53.8 is measured up-string off the SW post (tab §6 B38 / 1.6 §3), not from the north rim like every NS_STATION — it converts to station 84.2 on the N-rim chain. Reading it as 53.8 would put the TAB 15.95 in on the wrong side of post 6. The conversion is asserted against the frozen sibling ring study’s own figure.
⭐ THE COMMON PANEL — what is true of all four
  • Gravity is by BEARING, everywhere. Wood to wood, through full footprints. The project’s all-bearing rule is not a preference here; it is what lets flat straps be legitimate on rough true-4 stock at all.
  • Hardware resists SEPARATION and UPLIFT only. No strap, screw or plate on this page carries a pound of gravity. A screw-only base (an SDWS toe pair) is not proposed as the tie — an inclined screw resists uplift in withdrawal-dominated action, the exact class the F7 purge removed.
  • Rough true-4 stock takes FLAT hardware only — no formed saddles. That is the J3/HUCQ lesson, and it is why every tie here is a flat strap.
  • Green hemlock ⇒ ZMAX/G185 straps + HDG/SD fasteners, and fasteners clustered at the joint line (2.6a §6.4 green-shrinkage detailing).
  • ⛔ All four details are PROPOSED. The PE confirms. geometry.CONNECTIONS carries J12 (ridge post base → bearing chain) and J15 (ring post base → deck bearing chain) both as PE TO SPECIFY, and it says in terms that the seat detail below the floor “is stated by NO source”. Nothing in the proposals memo changes those statuses, and nothing on this page does either.
  • ⭐ J14 is marked where it belongs — and it is NOT a base. Where a ring plate meets a continuous post, nothing bears on the post’s top (v6 rule D), so the plate side-frames into the post face: that is J14, six joints, one application, PE TO SPECIFY, named by no source. It occurs at the tops of the four ridge posts, never at any base on this page. Do not confuse the two asks.

  5. ⚠ No ring post has a computed demand. P7’s bearing check runs on a bounding 1,500 lb corner reaction; the ring posts’ actual reactions are not computed anywhere. Domain B row owed — and it would come with the north-plate and south-collector rows the ring already owes.
  6. ⚠ Post 6’s bearing is FIELD-PENDING twice over — the as-driven beam line under the footprint, and the NOMINAL, gated TAB 14.45 in south of it. FIELD VERIFY.
  7. ⚠ R34 tape items: the nailer faces vs the cross centrelines at both ends, and the W-beam line at station 69.75. Documentation, not blockers — the model no longer pretends the crosses are the reference. FIELD VERIFY.

The full cathedral porch

The owner’s proposal: the porch region — stations 16 to 43.5, north of the door wall — fully open and unobstructed from the deck floor to the rafters. Concretely, the two north gable-line ring-plate segments are deleted, so nothing crosses the porch’s north face at Z 66. He saw the 5'-6″ plate over the north nailer in the frozen triangle study and rejected the headroom. This page draws it, and works the consequences honestly — including two the proposal did not name.

⛔ WHAT IS PROPOSED, AND WHAT IT AMENDS. If adopted this amends datum v10 rule A — the R32 ring — and needs a v11 Fable pass. It is labelled that way throughout. Deleted: the two station-16 gable plate segments (GABLE_PLATE_SEG_W 5'-6 1/2" + GABLE_PLATE_SEG_E 3'-1 1/2"), and with them the gable triangle above and everything that stood in it. Kept at the north face: the N-GABLE ridge post (continuous, 127.9 lb); the NW and NE corner posts (R30 solid rough 4×4, now carrying the eave plate ends); and, per the owner, “associated supporting NW/NE 16-oc framing up to the rafters” — read here as a narrow framed strip at each corner, the middle of the face fully open. ⛔ No source states the strip width. It is drawn ILLUSTRATIVE and tagged OPEN; the owner rules it.
⭐ The headroom it buys, at the ridge line: 5'-2" → 8'-11 5/8" — a gain of 3'-9 5/8". And a band 7'-8" wide where a six-foot adult clears the ceiling standing up. Under the deleted plate that band is zero: the plate’s underside is 5'-2" across the entire face.

⑥ The headroom won

The cathedral ceiling over the porch is the rafter soffit plane — the plane through the birdsmouth seats — except across the ridge beam’s own 4-in footprint, where the 10-in beam hangs below the rafters and is the ceiling. That is 2.12 §9.2’s own headroom rule: you measure to the beam soffit, because wood hangs below the beam top. ⛔ Z_APEX 120 is a seat-line construction point and geometry.py forbids printing it as a soffit apex — the trap the R20-held door memo fell into. The drawn soffit apex is 9'-10" at X 68.46, and a build guard refuses the page if it is not below Z_APEX.

⑦ Enclosure — one line, and it is the frozen sibling's

Under the owner’s stated reading 1 (the envelope closes at station 43.5, so the covered porch bay is outside it — his working assumption, carried as a PE-confirm line into brief v3), the openness of the station-16 face appears in no term of the ASCE 7-16 §26.2 test — not Ao, not Aoi, not Ag, not Agi. That is unchanged from the frozen triangle study, which worked the test on both live readings; nothing on this page re-opens or re-computes it, and no classification is claimed. Under reading 2 the aperture can only grow, so the proposal lands on the same side of that study’s condition-(1) straddle as its options (a) and (b) — which is exactly why the study handed the reading itself back as NEEDS_CONTEXT, PE/AHJ.

⑧ ⭐⭐ TWO CONSEQUENCES THE PROPOSAL DID NOT NAME

Finding 1 — the roof sheathing’s north edge loses the member it was going to be nailed to

2.6a §6.6 deliberately re-struck the rafter layout so that no rafter falls in a gable plane — the last rafter sits 5 in inboard of this line (4.625 in as tabulated on the drawn 121.25-in chord; R33-D flipped the basis of record to 122, which re-derives 5 — DERIVED HERE) so that both gable walls die into the sloped ceiling. The proposals memo is explicit about the consequence: the triangle’s top boundary “is therefore the roof sheathing plane itself, not an end-rafter soffit,” and the member that supports it is the raked cap on the gable studs — which is also, in P10, the roof diaphragm’s boundary member on the gable line.

⛔ This proposal deletes the studs, so it deletes the raked cap across the open middle of the face. What is left at that edge is the last rafter 5 in inboard, the 6" NOMINAL furring rake cantilevering past the line, and whatever barge or raked-cap treatment is chosen — and that treatment therefore becomes the entire diaphragm boundary story at this edge, where under P10 it was one member among several. P10 asks the PE for 8d at 6 in on boundaries plus 4 in o.c. within 48 in of roof edges and at gable-end framing, on this workbook’s own adopted Exposure C. That nailing needs something to go into.

⛔ NEEDS_CONTEXT — PE. No source on file specifies the replacement, and none is invented here: not the member, not its span (the same 5'-6 1/2" / 3'-1 1/2" the deleted plate had, now sloped and with only the corner strips under it), not its bearing, not its nailing. Figure 2 says so on its own face. The related standing gaps are already the workbook’s: §12h item (4) leaves the chords “by default”, §14.7 records the porch-region edges as “UNCHECKED and UNNAMED”, and §14.8 records that plate-to-stud uplift ties have no device, fastener or schedule specified.

Finding 2 — the N-GABLE ridge post loses the only member that ever framed into it at mid-height

9_TH_POST_RIDGE takes each ridge post’s length as “the LOCKED plate height 5'-6″” — an admitted proxy, recorded as such in geometry.py’s datum v6 rule D. The frozen post-bases study quotes the consequence: le/d 16.5, axial 0.094, bearing governs, not buckling.

The proxy predates the ring, so the ring did not create it — but the ring did make it true, at both gable lines: J14 puts a plate end into the post’s side at exactly Z 66. ⭐ Deleting the north segments withdraws that member, and station 16 becomes the one gable post whose modelled length has nothing behind it. Geometrically the unbraced height in the E–W direction goes from the modelled 66 in to the post’s full 107.635 in — le/d 16.5 → 26.91, DERIVED HERE and nothing more than arithmetic on RIDGE_POST_FLOOR_TO_SOFFIT and POST_W.

⛔ No capacity is computed on this page and none may be read into it. Two things are worth saying alongside it, both of which point the same way: this is the lightest of the four ridge stations (127.9 lb against 959.9 at the south mid), and the corner strips — whatever their ruled width — do not reach the ridge post, which stands in the open middle. So this reads as a margin question, not an alarm. It is a Domain B row to re-run on the honest length and a PE item, and it belongs on the v11 list.

A recommendation · a ruling · any selection between the proposal and the v10 ring · the corner-strip width · the corner posts’ top condition · the roof-edge boundary member, its span, its bearing or its nailing · a connector, part number, size, count or capacity for the plate-end-to-post joint or for anything else (the AC4RZ / BC4R family is named as under verification and nothing more) · a utilisation, a reaction or an allowable for any member · an enclosure classification · a price · a J-row · a component-registry ruling · a datum edit of any kind · any correction to calcs.xlsx, geometry.py, the proposals memo or any register · any modification of the three frozen sibling studies, which are quoted only.

Guards

build_study.py refuses to write the page if any of these fail, and names the offender:

  • ⭐ the datum gate — geometry.py’s banner must still read DATUM v10, read off the banner itself
  • ⭐ the premise gate — PLATE_W = PLATE_DEPTH = POST_W = 4.0, PLATE_STEP = 0
  • ⭐ the thing being deleted must still exist — the gable line must close, 66.5 + 4 + 37.5 = 108 exactly, and the two clear spans must still be 62.5 and 33.5, or this page is about nothing
  • the members that remain must remain: the ridge post continuous past the plate at all four stations, the eave plate length model untouched, and the west ladder entry still at 26.25 in ≥ the 24-in allowance
  • ⛔ the drawn soffit apex must sit below Z_APEX, which geometry.py forbids drawing as a soffit apex
  • ⭐⭐ the ceiling model — the rafter soffit must be above the ridge-beam soffit at both beam faces (or “the beam is what you stand under at the ridge” is false), the ceiling must rise monotonically from each eave toward the beam, and the printed gain must equal beam soffit less plate underside exactly
  • ⭐ the headline must still be a headline — the plate underside must still sit below 6 ft (so “nowhere on the face clears six feet today” is true), the 6-ft band must land inside the wall span, and a higher clearance must buy a narrower band. If any of that stops holding the page is rewritten, not re-run
  • ⭐ the roof edge — no rafter may fall in the gable plane (2.6a §6.6's re-strike is what makes finding 1 real), the inset must derive 4.625 on the drawn chord and 5 on the ruled basis, and the rake must reach past it
  • ⭐ the slenderness fact — the full post must be more slender than the modelled proxy, and the proxy must still be le/d 16.5; the guard is on the geometry only, because no capacity is computed
  • ⭐ handedness — all three figures put EAST on the right, deliberately, so they read together: Figure 1 looks NORTH from inside the porch (an exterior north elevation would be its mirror — the A-201 view-direction ambiguity, stated rather than assumed), Figure 2 looks NORTH, Figure 3 is a plan from above with north up; and up is up in both elevations
  • every SVG label measured against its own viewBox, horizontally and vertically, on a deliberately generous character-width table; every wrapped caption measured to a line budget so nothing breaks mid-word
  • a forbidden-claim scan (no adoption, no selection, no capacity, no classification, no connector named as chosen, and v11 may never be asserted as a fact) and a required-phrase scan (PROPOSED · FIELD VERIFY · PLANNING — NOT FOR CONSTRUCTION · the datum · the freeze rule · DERIVED HERE · never-invent · NEEDS_CONTEXT · Domain B · R21 · R28 · R30 · R32 · R34 · P1 · P2 · P10 · J13 · J14 · 2.6a · 1.2e · 9_TH_EAVE_W · owner rules)
